This research investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for obtaining approximate solutions to high-dimensional Schrödinger equations, where the goal is to compute eigenvalues and associated eigenfunctions. By measuring the generalization error in the input space, we derive finite-sample bounds that demonstrate how the error behaves with respect to certain parameters, such as input dimension, number of samples, architecture complexity, and other factors. A key aspect of our findings involves the analysis of architectural complexity in the context of high-dimensional spectral problems. We define architectural complexity as the product of the logarithmic values of the input space size and the number of output spaces, along with a boundary multiplier. A main conclusion of our research reveals that sufficiently large samples can lead to narrow generalization error bounds, even in high-dimensional settings where the input space is of the order of 10^6 or 10^9, among other dimensions.

In computational neuroscience, modeling neuronal activity with recurrent neural networks has been successful, particularly with datasets from the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome. This model's components, including neurons and their connections, operate in distinct time frames. To better understand and create effective models, researchers must analyze and interpret neuronal activity over varying time periods. Time series analysis is a valuable method in neuroscience for summarizing and understanding dynamic biological systems. We applied several time series metrics to simulate and analyze various computational neural models, ultimately finding that only one type of network successfully captured the complexity and variability of real neuronal data.

For the boundary value problem BVP associated with a planar rational harmonic function, around each singular point, the local behavior can be described by a certain power series. However, around points of infinite multiplicity, the power series expansion may not even exist. In response to this, recent research conducted by Alves, Monti and Zinn approach this issue by studying the near behavior of solutions using an extension of the Hardy operator. In the present study, the region around an arbitrary multiple infinite point of a certain nonlinear equation, where solutions exhibit asymptotic behavior, is determined. Specifically, the near behavior is found to be a stable manifold, which arises from the decomposition of the equation into its linear and constant components, given that the linear component corresponds to a certain non-degenerate irreducible cone.

A robust Gelfand pair (G, K) is defined by a group G and subgroup K where the double coset space has a specific property; it can be represented as the disjoint union of individual double cosets, corresponding to irreducible representations of G that possess a specific positive dimension. In the case of SL(2,p), our study focuses on finding robust Gelfand pairs within this group of prime order, especially irreducible irreducible pairs (SL(2,p), S(\Lambda)) where S(\Lambda) represents a p-specialization of the integer-coefficient symmetric group. Our primary finding includes a robust Gelfand pair (SL(2,p), Sp(1,p)) where Sp(1,p) is the p-th symmetric group, along with a robust Gelfand pair (\omega \otimes SL(2,p), \omega \otimes Sp(1,p)) where \omega represents a multiplicative group of roots of unity. Additionally, our study also demonstrates a robust Gelfand pair (SC(2,p), in both robust Gelfand pairs (SL(2,p), S\widetilde{Sp}(1,p)) and (SC(2,p), Sp(1,p)) where SC(2,p) is the 2nd symplectic group over p.

This research explores how the discovery of a $P$-wave, strangeness-lacking, hidden-charm molecular pentaquark in the $D^*(D^*\Xi)$ state impacts the existing understanding of molecular pentaquarks. The study reveals that, if the $D^*(D^*\Xi)$ state is a resonance with a decay width less than 5 MeV, it would challenge the commonly assumed $D^*$ and $\Xi$ magnetic moments. Specifically, if the $D^*(D^*\Xi)$ state is a resonance with a decay width of 5 MeV, it would require that the $D^*$ has a same-gauge factor of $-0.65\pm 0.18$ and the $\Xi$ has a same-gauge factor of $0.22\pm 0.17$. Additionally, this resonance would necessitate a modification to the currently accepted $\Xi$ magnetic moment. Similarly, if the $D^*(D^*\Xi)$ state is a broad resonance with a decay width of 100 MeV, it would necessitate a modified $D^*$ same-gauge factor and $\Xi$ magnetic moment. The study also notes that, in the event that the $P$-wave, strangeness-lacking, hidden-charm molecular pentaquark in the $D^*\Xi^*$ state is a resonance, it would require that the $\Xi^*$ has an electric

This is resolved by demonstrating that any non-abelian Zinbiel algebra necessarily contains a non-zero element a such that a squared product with any element b from the algebra generates a one-dimensional ideal.

We examine a finite, two-dimensional discrete torus where agents move randomly and reproduce, dying off only when they reach a specified maximum population size. Each new born agent is placed adjacent to its parent, and it has a diminished chance of surviving due to increased population density. In addition to movement and reproduction, agents also contract and pass on a disease, which reduces their reproductive potential. In this framework, we explore the long-term behavior and distribution of the population and disease across different states. We demonstrate the existence of a phase transition in a simplified model, and our method can be applied to other related problems such as diffusion, reproduction, and disease dynamics. By adapting existing work on diffusion, our findings offer insights into the natural clustering of diseases as well as the natural dispersal of information. In particular, we derive equations that describe the evolution of diseases and information in a simplified model, which can be applied to more complex scenarios where agent movement is influenced by disease distribution. For the latter scenario, we establish conditions that ensure the second moment of a wave function remains bounded, which in turn enables us to demonstrate the existence of a phase transition and derive specific critical exponents for certain wave function averages.

To study planets in intricate multi-planet systems, understanding their orbital harmonics is crucial, particularly in scenarios where planetary periods interact significantly. The multi-transiting planetary system K2-138, comprising six planets, posed an initial challenge in characterizing its orbital period ratios, which required careful observation of chaotic dynamics. Our analysis of TESS observations confirmed a predicted period sequence linked to the 3:2 resonance cycle, culminating in the verification of five orbital period ratios, including the novel identification of Pd3:2 in the 3:2 resonance, which sheds new light on the orbital period ratios of this complex planetary system.

We establish connections between the module category of the immanant algebra associated with $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ and the representation theory of $\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{gl}_n)$ via two functors: 
    1. A composition functor reflecting the quantum corresponding to classical duality.
    2. A functor linking the module category of the immanant algebra to the irreducible yet infinite-dimensional module of the quantum affine $\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{gl}_n)$, which we call the authentic Whittaker module. 
The established functors encompass the quantum affine analog of Euler's homogeneous function theorem and a generalization that incorporates Crainic--Prescott's work on immanants in cohomology. 
We prove under certain conditions that a specific authentic Whittaker module is semisimple, providing the desired objects for the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality correspondence. 
Our construction also encompasses the quantum affine analog of the Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial related to James' rank variety.

The SiD detector concept, initially designed for the ILCDM SuperB project, showcases a versatile and innovative approach to particle detection, with a phasic flow of hit data from various components to ultimately create a precise particle trajectory. This paper revisits the SiD sensor concept to optimize data processing and refine the particle reconstruction process within the context of the ILC's future.

Research on amorphous ices has sparked interest due to their unique properties, observed below 70 K, where liquid behavior coexists with solid-like attributes. Our investigation focuses on probing amorphous ice's structural integrity using ultrasonic measurements at 76 K, a temperature above the onset of solid-like behavior. Additionally, acoustic properties allow for probing both the elastic and viscous components within these materials. Our results reveal that at 76 K, amorphous ice displays an unexpectedly low storage modulus and high loss factor, indicating the presence of extensive 'liquid-like' domains. Moreover, when subjected to external pressure, these domains rapidly shift towards higher frequencies, causing a significant reduction in storage modulus and increased loss factor, characterizing the material as strongly dissipative. Ultimately, these findings highlight that crystallization rather than traditional liquidization processes govern amorphous ice's phase transition at temperatures and pressures resembling Earth's environmental conditions.

A computational model of Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy is employed to investigate the electronic structures of three materials:  bulk Graphite, Gold, and Silicon. Using this model, three key parameters are defined to characterize the Electronic Local Density of States of each material, effectively mapping the energy and momentum of each material's electrons. These parameters include the Local Density of States integration, Low Energy Variance, and High Energy Variance. It has been demonstrated that these parameters can distinguish between the Electronic Local Density of States of Graphite, Gold, and Silicon. Furthermore, the model allows for the differentiation between the (1x2) Graphite surface phase and the metallic (KK') phase, even at low energy levels. Additionally, the model enables the identification of the (4 T1g x 2) Gold surface phase, even at low energy levels. A possible explanation for the model's differentiation between the metallic (KK') and (4 T1g x 2) phases in Gold, and the higher Low Energy Variance and High Energy Variance in Silicon, is that these phases and states are reflective of distinct band formations in these materials.

In the last 40 years, the trusty Isabelle/HOL proof system has gathered a substantial 6588 important theorems, set out in  6643 separate files across 6643 separate directories. This proof system's extensive collection represents over four decades of collaborative work by numerous researchers. Our project focuses on examining and contributing to this remarkable corpus of formal proofs, examining how individual proofs are established and exploring their underlying structure, with an emphasis on identifying potential areas for improvement. By examining proof patterns, we aim to identify not just individual flawed steps but also potential sources of errors within the proof structure itself, ultimately guiding the development of more reliable and efficient verification tools for critical systems. Our research delves into the fundamental nature of formal proof validation, proof-testing, and proof-longitudinal monitoring, with direct relevance to the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs. Through thorough analysis, we have identified a total of 244 errors within the archive, carefully verifying their correction and offering suggestions for further improvement. In addition, we have made  6643 individual proof steps available for automated examination, enabling the analysis of Isabelle's proof strategy and the exploration of tools to support the verification of sequential logical proofs.

Understanding the magnetospheric turbulence that occurs how and why has been greatly aided by recent advancements in satellite technology. These advancements enable the collection of precise data on the magnetic field fluctuations resulting from turbulent energy cascade processes. To further advance our knowledge in this field, researchers can build upon the findings of wave detection techniques used on Earth by developing an instrument that can listen for the sounds of magnetospheric turbulence. This listening device would remain inactive until it detects a significant variation in current sheets, thereby allowing it to target and focus on specific areas. Furthermore, recent simulations have confirmed that ULF wave generation is loud enough to be detectable, albeit not quite loud enough to be heard. Consequently, all that is needed is a refined sensor and an updated design for a fully functioning magnetospheric audiometer. This audiometer would serve a dual purpose: first, it would help scientists understand the magnetospheric turbulence by identifying its source, direction, speed, and variation, thus facilitating a better understanding of the turbulent energy cascade. Secondly, it would allow researchers to examine in greater detail the impact of turbulent motions on trapped particles, thereby enabling a more precise modeling of their behavior.

Our research presents specific rotating dilaton black membrane solutions when coupled with logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics. We calculate key thermodynamic properties, such as temperature, entropy, and entropy variation, for these solutions. Notably, we examine the conditions under which the second law of thermodynamics is satisfied for these rotating dilaton black membranes.

To improve the accuracy of text classification and retrieval, a recent breakthrough in the field calls for representing words within their semantic context, rather than isolating individual words. However, current models often overlook the semantic connections among words and the overall topic structure, which can lead to inefficient word representations. This article presents a novel framework for automatically extracting semantic patterns from unlabelled text and using them to project words onto a topic-sensitive space. The topic boundaries are discovered through a combination of semantic and syntactic clues, and simultaneously, the word representations are refined to highlight their central meanings. We achieve this by leveraging a declarative memory recall system, inspired by the biological process of human memory retrieval. The framework features a three-layer architecture: the Storage Layer, Retrieval Layer, and Query Layer. The Storage Layer comprises an associative network that preserves original writings, as well as a semantic word lattice derived from the frequency of co-occurring words and the syntactic patterns they form. The Retrieval Layer enables declarative recall of stored items by identifying sequences that share similar semantics, and the Query Layer allows for the retrieval of items similar to a query word or topic. The framework is evaluated on various datasets, and the results show that it effectively captures semantic contexts and enhances the representation of text, surpassing state-of-the-art models.

For any real number q, such that its absolute value is less than one, we explore the complete positivity of a specific type of map associated with a specific q. This map is linked to a specific multiplication factor on Hilbert space with a dimension of at least one. It has properties such that it maps the CCR factors to the CAR factors and vice versa. This map can also be expressed as the composition of two other types of maps that both have properties of complete positivity. The image of the CAR factors under this map is seen to be dense in the CAR(q) factor for the specific case where q is between zero and one.

A reformed semantics for GP 2 has been developed as a direct interpretation of its rules, offering a straightforward understanding of the language through derivation trees, which can be easily visualized. This new semantics provides a natural basis for various transformation techniques applied to GP 2, such as the small-step operational semantics constructed from the reduced rules of the original semantics. Utilizing a structural recursion-based efficiency approach, this new semantics effectively minimizes computation steps. When applied to GP 2's small-step semantics, this technique produces a minimization algorithm, which has been proven to yield the minimum number of steps. Furthermore, this new semantics serves as a starting point for semantic analyses, such as context and abstraction leakages, which need to be addressed in GP 2. Additionally, GP 2's new semantics facilitates the analysis of context upgrade mechanisms like the latest value variation of the context, which can be studied by expressing the small-step semantics using the new minimization algorithm.

The way a young star releases its disk is crucial in determining how much material is lost and how this affects the star's accretion. Two mechanisms are frequently used to describe this process - the disk breeze, which involves ions being lost due to strong ultraviolet radiation, and photoevaporation, which involves the heating of gas in a young star's disk. Both models have been supported by X-ray observations of young stars, including TW Hydrae, which show strong high-energy emission consistent with either mechanism. However, a recent, high-resolution radio telescope survey of the TW Hydrae system has identified multiple detectors and revealed that most of its emission does not come from the star itself but rather widespread low-energy emission. Analyzing this survey alone cannot determine which mechanism is at work, but future, high-resolution radio telescope surveys will be able to identify specific low-energy emission patterns created by the movement of gas in a young star's disk. This will help determine whether photoevaporation or the disk breeze is the more accurate model.

We address the factorization problem for specific variants of Chebyshev polynomials through the use of minimal equations involving cosines with small denominators. This leads to the derivation of new factorizations for certain Chebyshev polynomials of the third and fourth kinds. Additionally, we demonstrate how these outcomes can be applied to provide minimal polynomial factorizations for specific cycles in the discrete cosine torus.

The proposed symmetrical phase angle regulating (SPAR) transformer architecture, consisting of two-core configurations, supports stable operation during extreme disturbances by maintaining its positive sequence voltage and controlling the zero and negative sequence voltages in accordance with established safety standards for low and high level faults. In the case of high level faults, self-protection mechanisms automatically de-energize affected windings while maintaining voltage supply to other coils, thereby preventing damage and ensuring operator safety. In addition, the SPAR transformer's built-in protective mechanisms also enable the categorization of system faults based on factors such as ground fault location, magnitude, and type. This innovative approach represents a significant development over traditional safeguard measures which often result in disconnecting the entire transformer and offers a major improvement in terms of power loss reduction and system resilience.

To support the high data rates required by fifth generation (5G) services such as virtual reality and augmented reality, multiple input multiple output (MIMO) mmWave communications hold great promise. However, the limited bandwidth of mmWave and high variability in channel attenuation necessitate the use of multi-carrier modulation with high productivity. As a result, the risk of broadcast channel interference increases significantly, severely hindering network capacity. This problem can be addressed through multi-group broadcasting (MGB), which involves dividing users into distinct groups and only allocates subcarriers to each group, thus minimizing interference. Despite its potential benefits, current MGB methods are limited by their reliance on prior knowledge of user data to separate groups and ensure subcarrier allocation. This paper introduces a novel, low-complexity approach hybrid-encoding (Hyec) to facilitate MGB by using different encoding methods for individual users and combining them through low-rank matrix multiplication, creating a unique signal for each group. Numerical simulations demonstrate that Hyec outperforms alternative multi-carrier techniques by combining high rank and low noise margins, a characteristic that does not decay with growing numbers of users and groups.

A group is said to exhibit residual finiteness expansion if its set of finite quotients admits an increasing sequence of finitely generated subgroups whose corresponding quotient groups are all infinite and finitely presented. This note proves that any group possessing a similar sequence of quotients that are infinite, finitely presented, and hyperbolic is in fact a group with nearly exponential residual finiteness expansion. This classification is equivalent to saying its ascending sequence of quotients' volumes are proportionally increasing at a rate greater than the natural logarithm of the previous quotient's volume. Additionally, it is shown that any group exhibiting polynomial RFE can be characterized as a subgroup of either a surface group or a cocompact arithmetic group.

We lay out the structural integrity framework for an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam attached to a star-shaped graph in this presentation. To move forward, we calculate the fundamental tones and normal modes of this beam, and then apply a previously established criterion to determine the stability of these fundamental states. Notably, we demonstrate that even with symmetric symmetry in the beam's geometry and the graph's structure, it can become unstable in specific cases where the point of connection is not centrally located. Moreover, we show that when the beam's geometry and the graph's structure exhibit anti-symmetric symmetry, it is guaranteed to be stable. The findings from our study are supported by numerical simulations.

For the upcoming $r$-process experiments at the European Nuclear Physics Facility, accurate and precise mass measurements are crucial, with uncertainties expected to be on the order of 100 kiloelectronvolts or less. To meet the needs of these experiments and future nuclear physics investigations, we have developed a machine learning framework for predicting nuclear mass values. This framework incorporates a systematic analysis of known data and takes into account the uncertainties associated with neighboring nuclei. Using Bayesian statistics, we have generated a mass function that not only predicts nuclear mass but also estimates its uncertainty based on the mass of surrounding nuclei. We have utilized our algorithm to measure the mass of nuclei across the nuclear chart, concentrating on areas relevant to $r$-process investigations. The performance of this algorithm is evaluated using two metrics: the average absolute deviation and the root mean square deviation. Furthermore, we have investigated the influence of different weighted neural network architectures and the effectiveness of incorporating a systematic bias in the learning process.

High-precision measurement of the microwave radiation attenuation properties in sapphire is conducted with an unprecedentedly high sensitivity of better than one part per billion. By utilizing this measurement in a range just below the quantum critical point of 300 millikelvin, the microwave quality factor is observed to drop off at low temperatures due to Seitz activation, in accordance with the established theory. The study's findings result in the determination of the total point defect density as approximately 1.9 x 10^13 cm^-3, or roughly 7.5 x 10^10 cm^-3 for active defects alone, and further reveals the fundamental nature of microwave loss.

The capacity of metamaterials to manipulate light through changes in the surrounding medium, as opposed to their structure, has been relatively underutilized. In this study, the optical pull of metamaterials and conventional materials is compared based on bulk responses. By inducing subtle variations in the refractive index, the metamaterials exhibit a significantly higher pull compared to those with conventional properties, while showing minimal differences in their nematic and isotropic phases. This increased pull is attributed to the distinct mechanical properties of the trimer metamolecules which cause them to shift slightly when the surrounding medium changes, resulting in enhanced polarization-dependent pull. This unprecedented level of light manipulation has the potential to enhance high-contrast imaging, super lenses, and ultra-sensitive detection capabilities.

Two-Stage Robust Optimization (TSRO) models uncertainty through scenarios, assuming that uncertainty falls within a predefined set, or 'ambiguity set', representing various modes of uncertainty. Historical models have used computationally demanding methods to solve these problems, where computational requirements have exponentially increased. Our approach develops a new duality for TSRO, with a maximum computational requirement proportional to the size of the ambiguity set. This is especially beneficial when dealing with scenarios and uncertainty sets that cannot be easily computed, such as discrete combinatorial optimization problems, which have seen a surge in recent research as they pertain to various real-world applications. Our new duality offers significant improvements, with a computational requirement proportional only to the size of the ambiguity set, as opposed to the number of scenarios, making it highly effective. Our approach is validated through comprehensive numerical experiments designed to test various levels of uncertainty scenarios and ambiguity set types.

The diversity of data plays a significant role in the complexity of tasks and is irreplaceable in both urban and economic studies. This paper presents a comprehensive dataset, H4M, consisting of diverse data originating from multiple sources in the Beijing metropolitan area. The dataset encompasses detailed information on residents regarding income, education, employment, and housing, as well as the data associated with neighborhood streets, bus routes, and commercial ventures such as restaurants. The resulting dataset comprises 2,346 residents and 1,667 neighborhood streets, featuring over 100 data attributes. Analytical tasks are proposed to address essential queries in socioeconomic research. Access to this dataset is granted via an online platform, allowing for easy exploration. The dataset is presently in English and Chinese languages, providing the option to analyze either individually or simultaneously.

The term "Information Assimilation Service" symbolizes the process of consuming and understanding data from various sources. Visualizing the structure of data enables individuals to quickly grasp their components, and multiple visualization tools facilitate this comprehension. Nevertheless, analyzing vast collections of interconnected data remains a challenging task due to their complex visual representation. To address this issue, we present "VisEOS," a visual interface that assists the systematic analysis of vast dispersed ontologies and shared graphs, facilitating the discovery of hidden patterns within these complex data sets. Built on the principles of services and workflows, VisEOS streamlines data analysis by integrating various visualization tools in an adaptable and AutoIQ-driven framework. This interface empowers users to create and save their own analysis protocols, and these customized methods can then be used to process other disjoint data sets, all within a browser-based environment. By leveraging VisEOS, users can seamlessly move through multiple CoSEs to gain a more in-depth understanding of each data set, thereby initiating a collaborative process called "Guided Analysis File" to further analyze additional disjoint data sets, thereby initiating a collaborative process called "Guided Analysis File" to further analyze additional disjoint data sets.

In the field of software effort prediction, models frequently excel, but their applicability to similar projects is often unclear. Recent advances in neural networks for software effort prediction have drawn attention, with a particular focus on the transfer of knowledge from other projects. Although transfer learning has made headways in both computer vision and natural language processing, its implications and execution on graph-structured data remain understudied. This research delves into transfer learning for neural network-based effort prediction models, with a goal of better comprehending its benefits, obstacles, and requirements. Our investigation examines how to implement transfer learning through both quantitive and qualitative analyses. An online survey of 22 experts provided the foundation for our study, highlighting primary concerns related to transfer learning. Based on the survey findings, we developed and evaluated open-source code featuring two distinct neural network architectures for transfer learning, along with case studies using two widely distributed benchmark datasets for effort prediction. The code is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/SheilaS/Sheila_Survey_Seezoo under the organization Seezoo. Our study indicates that a well-tuned transfer learning approach can greatly reduce the need for retraining a new model on a given project, with the success heavily dependent on the similarity between projects. Moreover, projects sharing effort patterns are more suitable for transfer learning. In such cases, effort prediction models are likely to exhibit greater accuracy, regardless of the model's initial design. While applying transfer learning to such projects is beneficial, it is

E-commerce websites feature numerous products, making it a daunting task for consumers to find the information they need. Consequently, many visitors face difficulties, including deciding which products to view and which websites to navigate. Our proposed system addresses these challenges by providing personalized suggestions to consumers. First, we identify key product features and their associated values, which serve as the basis for our system's feature evaluation mechanism. Next, consumers' comparative interests are analyzed in order to determine the distinctness of each product based on its shared features and group identities. Finally, our system presents consumers with a customized list of products by taking into account the uniqueness of each product and its notable features. Our dual feature allocation model relies on a method for identifying products' distinct group identities and unique features, which in turn enables our system to determine the quantity of suggested features for each group and individual products. Our model extends the traditional Rapoport-Prade model to incorporate these two decisions. Our model's dual formulation allows for the optimization of results by setting the price of distinctness and unique features in accordance with the products' estimated scroll distance, which serves as an proxy for their relevance.

Disjoints problems involve determining whether a specific element is absent from every subset within a collection of excluded sets.  The straightforward Disjointness problem - simply calculating whether a binary vector contains a zero in all of its blocks - is typically considered one of the most efficient problems to solve. Yet, a novel proof presented here reveals a more complex underlying combinatorial theorem, and further demonstrates a transformed view of this problem that is applicable in data streams, achieving a remarkable $O(\log r)$ space reduction, a gain equivalent to the log of the number of possible values in the vector's field.  By breaking down Disjointness into simpler sparse local tests, this proof showcases a new theoretical theorem of potential importance, providing a fundamental understanding of the problem's easy-to-solve nature.

We've found that the spin susceptibility of Heisenberg magnets in a non-magnetic state has a unique dependence on momentum and that the spin stiffness also exhibits similar momentum variation characteristics. Both the spin stiffness and spin susceptibility have a common origin in the transverse magnetic memory cell, which is a virtual excitation of the magnetic field. Due to a specific non-linear variation in the transverse magnetic memory cell's dispersion relation, a dimensional reduction takes place in the spin stiffness and spin susceptibility, resulting in both becoming scale-free. Contrasting with the linear variation in the spin stiffness found in analytical models, our numerical calculations based on the Monte Carlo method have confirmed a nonlinear variation in the spin stiffness. Both the momentum-based exponent of spin stiffness and the momentum-based exponent of spin susceptibility were determined through our analysis of the momentum dependence of these parameters. Resultantly, our study challenges the concept of dimensional reduction in the spin stiffness and spin variability, and it appears that both these parameters exhibit scale-invariant behavior due to a unique non-linear variation in the transverse magnetic memory cell.

A novel approach utilizing multi-diffraction patterns is proposed to capture, manipulate, and read single atoms with high spatial and spectral precision. Utilizing an atom-diffraction pattern that emerges from a laser beam with a variable frequency, this method can determine the position of a single atom within an optical trap. The E2 atom-diffraction pattern exhibits distinctive minima and maxima that can be utilized for reading the atom's position through either interference or diffraction patterns, resulting in comparable resolutions. However, due to a reduced number of laser frequency settings required to encompass the entire optical trap radius, this method offers a superior option over conventional interferometry, showcasing its potential as a control technique for single-atom manipulation. Computer simulations indicate the capability of this method to detect atoms made up of various atoms, such as those comprising Rb and Ce, providing further evidence of its feasibility.

The half-Hall effect in a two-dimensional electron system with interactions and random impurities can be understood by expanding on the classical Hall conductivity formula. By calculating how interactions and disorder affect the electromagnetic response of the system, researchers found that the system's response to a magnetic field varies directly with the charge of the impurities. Notably, for systems containing ferromagnetic impurities, the linear Hall conductivity vanishes, while a finite nonlinear Hall conductivity remains, and its magnitude is dependent on the spin flip rate at low temperatures.

There has been a significant surge in research on patient breathing apparatuses due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with numerous studies focusing on respiratory devices to save lives.  Many patient-centered respiratory devices are driven by breathing, with their performance heavily reliant on dynamics when influenced by breathing patterns. Despite the critical role of breathing in these applications, current engineering design practices typically ignore dynamics when developed using direct transcription due to perceived nonlinearity and irregularity of the problems in question. This paper aims to tackle the limitations of ignoring dynamics in direct transcription, with particular emphasis on a specific case study involving dual-patient Venturi mask equipment. We also propose a new approach known as Dynamic Enhancement, where we combine different models to leverage the strengths of each and mitigate their individual shortcomings, with a key goal of ensuring the developed device meets "maximum" safety standards. This methodology first identifies and harnesses the most effective characteristics of each model, and then, based on specified criteria, selects and blends these components to create a comprehensive and optimized approach to device design. Furthermore, we also identify and incorporate relevant in-domain data, with a goal of adding robustness to the model. By applying this new approach to design dual-patient Venturi masks, our findings indicate that taking into account the dynamics of the problem in question leads to a substantial, statistically significant improvement in maximizing safety, with a very significant improvement in this regard, with results showing a 100% improvement over models without dynamics for certain critical measures such as "maximum"

We investigate group-theoretic properties of iteration maps associated with bicritical rational functions. Such functions have a mapping degree of $\mu$ with $\mu \ge 3$ and satisfy certain critical set conditions. Our focus lies in understanding the symplectic group platform of $f^k$, where $k$ is a positive integer and $f$ is such a bicritical rational function. Specifically, we derive a criterion for determining if a double vector $(V, q)$ supports a platform of $f^k$ as a $\mu$-fold cover of $\mathbb{C}^2$. This criterion extends earlier work by applying the Yosida decomposition to the Fitting lemma for the Jacobian matrix of $f$. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the Jordan normal form of $\mu$ and the Jordan normal form of the Lie algebra's $sp(T_V)$ symplectic structure. Our analysis covers all possible values of the mapping degree $\mu$, including the difficult case where $\mu = 3$.

Two-dimensional semiconducting devices and new discovery Mo and W dichalcogenides could be utilized in their single layer, few layer, or bulk form. The focus here is on the variation of their work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity with layer thickness. The calculations were performed for the entire range of their stable monolayers ($MO_2$), bilayers ($MO_2$)$_2$, three layers ($MO_2$)_3$, and bulk form - six layers in a supercell (S6) of Mo and W dichalcogenides using DFT theory with PBE exchange-correlation potential, and also using GW theory with PBE0 exchange-correlation potential. The results indicate a decrease with increasing layer thickness in their work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity. By computing the band gaps, the authors have verified that the layer thickness has minimal impact on the band gaps in dichalconides. The results indicate a good agreement between DFT and GW calculations for the two dichalconides in all forms - monolayers, few layers, and bulk. The layer-dependent changes in work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity could be attributed to the differing effective potentials derived from electrostatic, exchange, and correlation potential in space.

A novel, comprehensive algorithm is developed to resolve the challenging problem of supervised universal learning. Based on the fundamental concept of "selfness," this algorithm formally quantifies the self-referential relationship between a network's internal dynamics and the external dynamics of its input data. It is then substantiated that this "selfness" metric offers a universal learning criterion. Moreover, this algorithm is grounded in a contemporary information theory known as "information-field theory," which provides a sophisticated framework for modeling complex data systems and optimizing network dynamics. It is shown that optimizing a network's performance according to the "selfness" metric involves a process of iterative data-driven feedback loop closure, effectively enabling the transmission of external information into the network. Furthermore, this algorithm is demonstrated to be a precise implementation of the principles underlying "delta-lens" theory, a theoretical framework for developing universal learning systems. Specifically, it is illustrated that the algorithm can be expressed in terms of a sequence of "delta-lens" frames, each of which captures a fundamental learning paradigm: pattern matching, vector field alignment, and state transfer. Consequently, this algorithm offers a comprehensive framework for integrating and unifying diverse paradigms of supervised learning, as well as a fundamental theoretical foundation.

We develop an approach that enables the exclusive use of integration by parts to establish the uniform boundedness of Fourier multipliers with limited smoothness. As a result, this leads to a broad estimation technique for functions defined on compact sets of flat spaces with limited smoothness, which satisfies certain consistent conditions. In contrast to existing methods, this novel approach can handle the complex scenario where the domain is not convex. It is noteworthy that the smoothness requirement for our method is essentially a design constraint, as it could be satisfied even with very little smoothness – essentially 1. As a demonstration of our method's versatility, we prove phase estimate uniformity under the sole condition that it's constant.

A fast iterative method for two-dimensional rarefied gas simulation is introduced, using a gradient correction technique to iteratively refine the solution towards its equilibrium state. The method converges to the correct solution with high accuracy, in a small number of iterations, which increases with the Knudsen number but remains under 1000s even at very low Knudsen numbers. It is capable of handling complex scenarios, such as collective drag and flow around a moving solid, and is compared to an exact Boltzmann model for high accuracy and to a numerical model that assumes the gas has reached equilibrium. The method's high iteration efficiency is attributed to the use of an accelerated iterative strategy, which uses a prognostically-driven approach to update the gas model in real-time, as well as the use of a numerical model that accurately predicts the gas's behavior without overestimating it. This approach enables the simulation of physical effects at a molecular level, in a broad range of large-scale situations, from fluid dynamics to materials science and biology.

Researchers detected an anomalous phenomenon at the Horizon-10T observatory located on the Qingyang Mountain in China, capturing a multi-modal event featuring a primary signal followed by multiple harmonics. The investigation into this event focuses on the potential connection to Axion Quark Nuggets (AQN) decaying and emitting an extremely low-frequency geoneutrino radiation. Theoretical modeling of an event similar to the observed one shows that it could be part of a previously undiscovered low-frequency cosmic background similar to cosmic ray radiation. The likelihood of detecting this event multiple times by Horizon-10T relies on factors including the decay rate, mass, and the number of AQN in the vicinity of the observatory. Based on these assumptions, estimates suggest that Horizon-10T could detect this event around 0.01 times per year, which could be observable using a similar device or detectors capable of accurately measuring low frequencies.

Results from a likelihood ratio test, comparing observed two-photon data to predicted Higgs two-photon decays, place a 68% confidence limit of 83 - an unprecedentedly low limit for this process. Further CMS analyses using 13 TeV data have derived 95% confidence level upper limits per combination of spin parity and CP state for Higgs-like bosons, ranging from 83-77 GeV in mass. For studies applying combined spin parity and CP state to Higgs-like boson analyses, the following 95% confidence level upper limits per combination have been derived: 76-46 GeV in mass for spin-parity 0, and 84-53 GeV in mass for spin-parity 1 or a pure CP-negative state.

We examine the p-divisibility properties of the Fourier coefficients within Siegel modular forms, specifically focusing on the cases of half-integral weight and special elliptic modular forms connections.

This study establishes a precise sequence of commutative groups in relation to independent fibrations by employing a novel characterization of fibrations requiring minimal length, which is based on the concept of cable-like arcs with a specific length constraint. This characterization is shown to accurately describe commutative groups in relation to independent fibrations, thus resolving a long-standing conjecture first introduced by Artin and Zweck, and later further explored by Gromov, by demonstrating that the fibrations in question can be expressed as a sequence of symmetric group products with each subsequent group having a dimension at least twice of the preceding one.

The presence of Pauli blocking in the formation of two-dimensional Pauli crystals is crucial. A significant amount of research currently focuses on the electronic configuration of these structures, formed by the accumulation of opposing spin electrons in very weak magnetic fields. In contrast, our analysis explores the thermodynamic stability of these structures, strongly influenced by entropic factors near the Fermi level. A comprehensive mathematical model has been created to illustrate the system's energy levels and entropy. This framework demonstrates that Pauli blocking alone is not enough to explain the emergence of these crystals and highlights a more complex interplay between thermal and magnetic properties within the system. As such, this study suggests a revised perspective on the subject is necessary.

Highly fluctuating data characterize many real-world problems in science and engineering. Nonetheless, traditional neural networks struggle to handle the time-varying nature of the underlying matrices in these issues. The zeroing neural network (ZNN) approach was developed to tackle this challenge, aiming to solve time-dependent matrix problems proactively using a stable, asymptotic solution. Since its introduction, ZNN has proven effective in addressing a variety of problems, such as matrix inversion, roots finding, and differential equation integration. The ZNN framework is versatile, applicable to both discrete and continuous data sets, and flexible, accommodating the use of bases, parameter learning, and convolutional structures. The presented paper provides a comprehensive overview of ZNN, including its underlying theory, numerical implementation, and recent applications. A selection of example algorithms is included to illustrate the framework's components, accompanied by a review of ZNN-based studies in the literature.

Deep neural networks excel at computer vision tasks, but their complex structures render their visual perceptions unclear. Research has shown that similar patterns often receive similar responses from most convolutional networks, which raises concerns about their ability to effectively learn image features. To investigate the visual perception capabilities of a novel network designed with simplified convolutions, we developed a perceptive field model consisting of on-off, center-surround structures. Our model, called OSCS-Net, not only outperformed state-of-the-art models in classification tasks, but its sparsity and modularity also significantly reduced inference time and memory usage, making it more efficient for image processing. Furthermore, the model's improved prognosis, which is based on an ablation study, suggests that its effectiveness stems from its ability to perform convolutions with both uniform and non-uniform information, particularly in its ability to effectively process edge information. These conclusions demonstrate the importance of developing neural networks with simplified convolutions that mimic natural visual processes.

Upcoming space missions need high-resolution X-ray telescopes covering a broad field-of-view, although such specifications are economically difficult to achieve. We propose employing various techniques to enhance the optical design of X-ray telescacles, including using twisted, bent, and offset reflectors as well as focusing arrays with different concentrations. These techniques can increase the field-of-view while maintaining a high resolution, and we provide numerical examples of these methods. Furthermore, we examine the feasibility of employing these techniques in future space missions and discuss potential challenges and advantages.

The presence of spatial charge variations in twisted bilayer graphene is effectively described by a two-dimensional model incorporating a topological term. Applying a homogeneous magnetic field gives rise to a dependence on its orientation $\phi$ in the model's Hamiltonian. This results in the occurrence of reentrant, flat energy levels in low-energy Landau bands that demonstrate periodic fluctuations with the angle $\phi$. The number of such levels increases as the number of involved Fermi levels decreases, in accordance with a modified version of the Berry-Symmetry-based Floquet magnetization theorem, where local magnetization behavior is governed by the Berry curvature in the model's single-particle band structure. This suggests the potential for controlling the spin of carriers through an electric field for purposes such as room-temperature spintronics in twisted bilayer graphene.

Inspired by a desire to hide one's intellectual endeavors, we propose a novel form of text-based steganography. Leveraging the capabilities of LSTMs to recognize patterns, we have developed a system for encoding secret information within ordinary-looking text and demonstrated its effectiveness at detecting such hidden content. This approach for steganography boasts a significant advantage in terms of concealment relative to previous implementations. Additionally, we have made our code and parameters readily accessible for optional fine-tuning.

The way power plants are operated on the electricity network is being changed. Instead of buying at the lowest available price, a balance between maintaining the quality of the energy supply and the environmental impact is now being considered. However, incorporating these new factors into the energy distribution systems has raised complex planning issues regarding how to manage and optimize power plant operations effectively. To resolve this problem, a model has been developed to simulate the costs and consequences associated with different operational approaches, which can be used to identify constraints quickly and find the most efficient solutions efficiently. The model has been tested and found to reduce computation time dramatically, allowing it to be used in real-world applications. The results show a high level of accuracy, which is on par with more comprehensive models, and can be used as a starting point for more in-depth planning. The model has the potential to not only optimize power plant operations but also provide guidelines for managing flexibility in the energy supply.

We conducted ab initio Monte Carlo studies to investigate how different external pressures affect antiferromagnetic ordering in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$. Our findings suggest that dimerization, resulting from $JJ'$$ structure transformation is triggered by pressure-induced $J'$ shortening but does not necessarily lead to it. Antiferromagnetic long-range order is stable under pressures below 12 GPa but disappears completely above 18 GPa, where dimerization is more extensive. Long-range order is reestablished when the distance between iridium ions is minimized, resulting in the structural transformation typical of higher pressure Li$_2$IrO$_3$ compounds.

The synthetic control method has become a crucial approach for small sample causal inference in contemporary empirical research. This two-stage method involves using a set of indicator variables to isolate treatment effects based on a weighted combination of pre-intervention treated and control group data. The weights are determined by comparing the treated unit to a combination of control units, known as the synthetic control. This method yields an unbiased estimate of the treatment effect only if the weights are chosen correctly, a task that poses significant challenges in small sample settings. As a result, there is a need for a more systematic approach to selecting weights that leverages knowledge about the data. This study develops a framework for weight selection called Proximal Causal Analysis, incorporating ideas from proximal optimization, gradient boosting, and network analysis. The proposed framework is not only computationally efficient but also provides direct and informal suggestions for weight selection that can be interpreted causally. The Study evaluates the performance of Proximal Causal Analysis using two case studies, 1) a simulated model and 2) a real-world dataset analysis related to Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) in the US, showing that it not only yields unbiased estimates but also achieves significantly lower average losses when compared to traditional SCC approach.

In recent years, there has been a significant rise in applying network representations to a variety of disciplines. To address concerns of data security and compliance with GDPR, there is a growing need for secure and reliable analysis tools that can preserve the sensitive information of individuals while still allowing for meaningful statistical inferences to be drawn. This project leverages the Gromov-Wasserstein divergence to perform a secure and private analysis of distributional networks. To ensure the analysis meets the requirements of differential privacy, we integrate the GW-divergence into the framework of the Laplace mechanism. Specifically, we formulate the secure estimation of a GW-distribution as an optimization problem that minimizes a proxy divergence between the estimated distribution and the actual distribution. This optimization is performed across multiple nodes in a distributed manner using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). We demonstrate that this approach meets the requirements of $\epsilon$-differential privacy and provides robust results that are in line with the underlying data. Furthermore, we apply the newly developed framework to analyze a real-world dataset consisting of anatomical brain connections across different individuals.

Recent high-energy laser-wakefield acceleration experiments have used extremely powerful lasers to produce a groundbreaking achievement of multi-GeV electron acceleration in a single meter. When operating in the plasma, these experiments inherently involve complex interactions between the laser and the plasma, influenced by its inherent gradations of electron density. However, the standard model used for analysis assumes a uniform plasma, which often leads to inaccuracies in interpreting the results. To rectify this limitation, a new study has taken into account how lasers with a particular type of intensity gradient interact with the plasma. It's discovered that this intensity gradient affects how electrons are injected and accelerated by means of a unique nonlinear electrostatic field that arises in the plasma, aligned at a 45-degree angle to the direction of propagation. Furthermore, the experiment shows that electrons are frequently injected at an angle due to this field, which the researchers have explored in detail. Additionally, the investigation considers how the polarization of the laser impacts the electron acceleration by demonstrating that anisotropic electrostatic fields generated by the laser's polarization can accelerate electrons at an angle, giving rise to distinct optical patterns in the electron beam's transverse electric field that are dependent on the polarization.

A sophisticated detector design utilizing platinum foils and X-ray arrays has been developed to set more precise boundaries on various decay processes and check for dark matter interactions. The revised version of our most sensitive measurement to date of the double beta decay of platinum has been conducted, yielding a more stringent limit on this process. A subatomic sensitivity threshold was achieved while measuring the platinum radioactive decay network. Furthermore, our study investigated the possibility of dark matter interactions in platinum using a novel technique involving relaxation of nuclear levels and observation of unusual events. Our research set more accurate bounds on relevant interaction models, including GeV-scale spin-dependent and spin-independent models, as well as axion-like particles with couplings to electrons.

The calculation of the renormalization group evolution of the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge, responsible for the properties of hadrons such as the neutron's spin depression and the rho meson's helicity, is carried out in dimensional regularization for a general number of flavors. This calculation reveals the relationship between the singlet axial-vector current and the anomalous magnetic moment of the rho meson, and how it is influenced by gluon condensates. A critical component of this calculation is the computation of the QCD axial-vector current anomaly, involving a thorough evaluation of the relevant hexagon integrals. This work draws heavily from previous studies on the renormalization of the electromagnetic current in QCD.

Dynamic camera filtering techniques adjust camera sensitivity in real-time to
achieve visually appealing results, however current methods are limited to a
single camera, unable to take advantage of multiple cameras or simulate matrix
capture. This work introduces a new cross-camera input technique that allows for
 seamless image processing across multiple real-world cameras with varying
characteristics, without the need for manual calibration. This innovation
enables smooth transitions between cameras, accurate subject tracking, and a
richly textured matrix effect, all of which are highly valued in cinematography.
Furthermore, our technology uniquely combines real-world cameras into a single
matrix image, a feature previously only achievable with specially designed
multi-camera systems or computer-generated simulations.

The paper presents a comprehensive study on various representations of the Lie symmetries and conservation laws associated with the generalized Ermakov system expanded from the fourth-dimensional model. It specifically explores a new method for translating Noether's theorem, allowing for the derivation of symmetries and conserved quantities based on equivalent variations of a Lagrangian density that has undetermined variables. This approach reveals that the generalized Ermakov system is galilean invariant and soluble via symmetry reductions obtained from the Lie point symmetry system. Seven distinct combinations of the conserved quantities were identified, which include four Noether conserved quantities from the expanded Lagrangian and three non-Noether conserved quantities from the equivalent Lagrangian density with variable $\mathbf{A}$. Moreover, the paper inquires whether the generalized Ermakov system's galilean invariance implies its invariance under the galilean transformation, and the answer is negative; in fact, one Noether symmetry and four non-Noether symmetries from the equivalent Lagrangian density with variable $\mathbf{A}$ confirm this result.

Public Transportation APIs have revolutionized the development of applications for passengers, researchers, and engineers, offering a wealth of real-time data. Despite its significance, feeding Specification data to machines remains a daunting task, with human-generated schedules and routes often incompatible with digital platforms. If properly formatted, this data can be instrumental in processing stop and route suggestions, fare calculations, and other functions. Drawing from the Transit Feed Specification, this project harnesses the potential of machine learning and reinforcement learning to create an innovative solution for processing TFS data. By training a recurrent neural network, this system can accurately parse complex feed data, with a high success rate of 0.859. Additionally, this system can also fill in missing fields in the feed and revert it to its original state, offering flexibility. Importantly, this solution does not necessitate human labeling of datasets, making it a more efficient option. Further research is required to enhance the feed's reliability and explore additional uses for the recurrent neural network.

In the field of few-shot classification, prototyping stands out as a highly effective technique. Currently, representative prototypes are generally categorized into category-based and graph-based types. However, we argue that a more natural and effective set of prototypes could be centered around categories, where the distribution of each class's data is taken as a prototype, mimicking the concept of clustering. We introduce the concept of 'class-type prototypes', where each prototype comprises multiple classes sharing similar characteristics. Our method, named MultiClassPrototyping, addresses the limitations of existing prototyping by implementing an autoencoder-based system that learns these class-type prototypes from the data. By doing so, we aim to create a system where each prototype encompasses a cohesive set of similar-looking classes, thereby utilizing these prototypes to accurately identify the target class when presented with novel few-shot verification tasks. Our method demonstrates a notable 14.2% improvement in accuracy relative to the existing state-of-the-art prototyping approaches, across the standard benchmarks for few-shot classification.

We're analyzing a class of non-reversible continuous symmetries, which can be a combination of two different types: one that doesn't change when transformed ($U$) and another that does change when transformed ($\bar U$). Our research explores the conditions under which these symmetry transformations will not be "broken", even in situations where they're "time-asymptotically irreducible". We've found that as long as certain "currents" related to the symmetry are "conserved, except possibly at initial times", both types of symmetry will be preserved. We've used this result to demonstrate that certain "global $U(1)$ dipole conservation laws" in both $SO(3)$-invariant systems and systems with $SO(3)$ non-reversible symmetry also imply the Poincar\'e symmetry is preserved, leading to preserved dispersion relations. This result is an extension of work previously done by $M\"ochen and Sonnenfeld$, which considered the $U$ symmetry only.

A graph G is termed split, when it can be divided into a discrete set of vertices χ and two separate, disjoint groups of vertices ρ and σ, with the condition that ρ and σ are respectively only linked to χ and not linked to each other except by the possible connection to a vertex in χ. A graph directional pattern is deemed semi-transitive when for any set of three vertices in the graph, the direction of connection from one to another only holds true if the connection from the first to the second also exists. This research explores semi-transitive graph direction in split graphs, determining the minimum number of directional connections required for a split graph to be semi-transitive. For graphs with more than three vertices in the discrete set, a split graph is semi-transitive with the minimum number of directional connections equal to the sum of the vertex total in the discrete set and one more. Furthermore, a corresponding non-constructive proof for the lower bound of directional connections required for a split graph has also been derived, specifically with the condition that the total number of vertices is three, in addition to the discrete set's total number of vertices, in this instance, two.

Identifying decay modes of tau particles, particularly those with hadrons, in high-energy physics experiments is increasingly difficult due to similarities between these decays and background processes, resulting in a high incidence of fake taus. A novel deep neural network is developed to distinguish real hadronic tau decays from those simulated with the same hadronic decay final states, utilizing a dataset from the LHCb experiment. This network achieves an acceptance rate of 77.1% for real taus while rejecting 95.1% of simulated taus decays, corresponding to a rejection rate that is approximately 3.4 times more efficient than a conventional strategy using a likelihood test. A deep neural network is now applied to an ongoing analysis involving hadronic tau decays in the LHCb experiment to reduce fake taus, with the goal of improving precision in particle physics measurements and searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.

Future deep sky surveys, notably the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, are projected to generate vast amounts of data, which includes photon counts that can be analyzed to obtain key morphological features and probabilities for galaxy classifications, star formation rates, and other measures. We investigate the feasibility of using a Bayesian Neural Network to classify star-forming and passive galaxies from H-alpha emission flux distributions by employing the Stingray package for data simulation, the PyTDM library for time-series analysis, and the Blobber library for probabilistic inference. Our study examines the impact of different observation times, durations, and frequencies on galaxy classification accuracy, with the findings showing that a short-duration (10-minute) observation with a high frame rate can achieve 90% accuracy and a low rate of 10% misclassification, with the latter resulting in an equal priority assignment to all outcomes.

Our study delves into the theoretical basis of the intermodal Brillouin scattering transfer in solid-core photonic crystal fibers (PCFs).  By adapting the fundamental mode's spatial beam expansion for high-order modes, we derive a model that forecasts the modal coupling via the Brillouin effect.  This phenomenon is characterized by the interaction between the fundamental mode and higher-order modes due to their differing phase and group-velocity matching.  Emerging research indicates that PCFs with a turnaround point at 1300 nm can facilitate near-doubling of the Brillouin gain through mode coupling, thus offering a high-efficiency optical Brunel engine.  Additionally, we found that for PCFs without a cutoff, the effective mode coupling occurs primarily with the fundamental mode, resulting in a simplified optical design for the engine.  This mode interaction offers a versatile technique for shaping the light beam and advancing modal diversity, presenting novel opportunities for fiber-based nonlinear optical applications.

The intersection lattice of positive roots in the weight lattice of a reduced affine
Borel subgroup of a algebraic group is isomorphic to the face poset formed from
reflections of the weight lattice, according to a theorem previously established for
type A_2 and A_n, with various other types addressed in subsequent studies.
This article demonstrates that a generalization of this theorem holds for the
B_n and D_n cases, while similarly, D. Stanislavov had previously found it also
applies to G_2. This article also establishes that a similar generalized theorem
holds for the classification of minimal elements in the intersection lattice of
positive roots, in addition to revealing an individual root from this lattice
corresponding to a 2-element subset of simple roots in B_n and D_n cases.

The Budgeted Maximum Coverage problem involves finding the most cost-effective solution to cover a specified number of items with the utmost efficiency. This combinatorial optimization problem has applications in several domains, including data mining and budget allocation. A related issue, the Set-Union Knapsack Challenge, also exists within this realm, where a machine's capacity can only process so many items before experiencing technical difficulties. To address these combined issues, a Local Search algorithm has been devised to provide an effective solution to these two problematic areas. This innovative approach iteratively selects a subset of items from a given dataset, ensuring that item coverage and total cost are effectively balanced to provide an optimal comprehensive solution. Using a straightforward removal and addition policy, this algorithm yields a productively optimal outcome to these two coverage issues. Our extensive experimental analysis, involving synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrates that this algorithm consistently produces a high-quality solution that surpasses existing competitive approaches within these two problematic areas. This algorithm has been successfully validated to provide an efficacious solution to these two coverage issues.

In this competitive and rapidly evolving field of online gambling, customer retention is crucial. We have developed an innovative attraction forecasting framework that integrates Attraction Reproduction and Time Series modeling for this purpose. Our system, ARATS, leverages an attractive state representation and a time series model to accurately predict attractions. By being a modular, online, and real-time solution, ARATS provides valuable support to operators in optimizing customer engagement.

Building on the foundational work by Yang and Lee, this text revisits the computation of the analytic continuation of the two-point correlation function of the Ising model's spin operators across the complex magnetic field plane. Enabling the correlation function's identification of the location and strength of the Yang-Lee discontinuity, this analysis employs both exact thermal excitation series and cumulative correlation length asymptotics to pinpoint the relevant parameters in the magnetic field regime of sub-critically positive values. Furthermore, this text presents new results from a numerical field theory approach that confirms the findings and provides the precise location and amplitude of the discontinuity.

The gluon transverse momentum dependent distribution functions are key components that explain the transverse momentum of hadrons produced in collisions and the spin correlations between them. Building on large-momentum effective theory and using renormalization group techniques, we derive the full set of TMD PDFs for gluons, which will help in better understanding gluon polarization in hadrons, producing gluons in collisions, and resolving issues in perturbative calculations.

This analysis examines the interaction of low-momentum electrons and positrons with heavy nuclei in high-energy collisions of heavy ions. Three production mechanisms for these leptons are considered: the creation of pairs, the photon-induced Breit-Wheeler pair production, and the interaction of electrons with large nuclei through transfer of nucleons. Calculations of lepton production in collisions of lead atoms at very low momentum are presented and discussed.

To develop comprehensive traffic risk management, precise and continuous assessment of cyclists' and motorized vehicle drivers' behavior is essential. Existing survey methods have notable limitations in gathering relevant behavioral data for large-scale urban areas. On the other hand, accurately detecting traffic behavior from video data can provide a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of all road users. There's nonetheless a shortage of suitable algorithms capable of detecting the behavior of all road users from video data in a cost-effective manner for general areas. Our study introduces a new approach, referred to as VBiRCD, to analyze traffic behavior from video data. Our system integrates a roadside camera's automatic tracking system with a behavioral analysis algorithm to describe and characterize the behavior of cyclists and drivers based on specific context. Our approach can describe behavior in two ways: visually, by identifying critical incidents such as reckless driving, and numerically, by assigning a risk score to cyclists and drivers based on their behavior. Our study demonstrates that VBiRCD's risk descriptor has a high correlation with real-world cyclist accidents in a comparative analysis conducted in four cities.

This research proposes a pioneering approach to robustly navigating robots in complex dynamic environments, using Motion Planning Control Barrier Functions to ensure safe and reliable trajectories. Our novel framework combines the limits of both motion planning and control barrier functions to tackle robots of any shape or type in any dimension. This method employs a pre-compiled database of precomputed motion paths that can be quickly retrieved and rapidly adjusted in real-time to prevent collisions or maintain stability. It does this by using the robot's current dynamics and a predicted simulation of its future state to set realistic and achievable goals for the path finding algorithm, which up to this point has limited capabilities. This process allows the robot to efficiently avoid obstacles in real-time, using a precomputed database of motion paths that can be quickly retrieved and updated. This allows the robot to efficiently avoid obstacles in real-time, with a 1000x speedup in processing times. This research utilizes the TrajOpt motion path finding algorithm but our framework can be applied to any type of algorithm or software. Our approach to robust navigation in dynamic environments has been implemented in a fully automated system that can be easily replicated on any robot.

For any ring R, the boundary numbers are defined as specific set-valued measurements: 
- The upper bound numbers u_R(V) for subsets V of R^2,
- The lower bound numbers l_R(V) for subsets V of R^2.
These boundary numbers represent variations in mappings from R^2 to itself that remain constant on congruent sets.
The boundary numbers of a ring R have several essential qualities and are closely connected to ideals in R.
Moreover, for any ring R, the boundary numbers satisfy certain boundary conditions.
Based on the boundary numbers, the categories Rad_R and Prim_R of rings are respectively defined by ideals in R that fulfill certain boundary conditions or have a single maximal ideal with this property.
The boundary numbers play a significant role in the structure and composition of these categories of rings.
Our research demonstrates a correspondence between the categories of rings with prime boundary numbers and the categories of semiprime rings in themselves.
The boundary numbers of a ring R can also be used to determine the height of left ideals in R, which leads to an innovative definition of the composition height of a ring R.
The composition height of a ring R has several crucial properties and is an essential characteristic for studying composition rings and free abelian groups in R.

Deep neural networks exhibit impressive performance across various tasks but are
vulnerable to manipulation by intentionally crafted adversarial inputs that cause
them to misclassify the correct outcome. Prior research mainly focused on the
predictability of specific tasks, whereas the current study aims to explore
resilience as a characteristic of models in general. Furthermore, we seek to
develop organic defenses that don't affect normal data processing, while also
investigating multiple forms of adversarial inputs and their respective impact
on our method's performance.

This paper presents an extension of classical Euler equations to nonlocal gas dynamics models, incorporating diverse target functions such as the Arzier, Bregman, Kullback-Leibler, and relative entropy functions. The extended models are analyzed in a broad range of spaces, including $L^2$ and Besov spaces of orders less than 5/3, with the transport being either general or aligned with the velocity field. The models satisfy the Kato-Opdam condition, ensuring a well-defined measure for the flux functions. The models are shown to have globally solvable solutions for short periods, which are Entropy admissible and fulfill the nonequilibrium entropy condition. The solutions' long-term behavior is also predicted, with or without the nonlocal parameter's influence. The models' behavior as the parameter approaches zero or infinity is examined, with the analysis confirming the expected behavior for commutative transports but presenting unexpected results for non-commutative transports, which show a phase transition at a transport order of 5/3. The results of this study provide the most comprehensive understanding to date of nonlocal gas dynamics models, which has led the authors to formulate questions and predictions for nonlocal parameter's behavior in a wide range of transports.

Dilation surfaces are a class of surfaces that arise in hyperbolic higher-dimensional dynamics, specifically as boundaries of polytopes in hyperbolic space. They exhibit smooth behavior under a specific unfolding process, which can be described by a Morse-Smale flow. This smoothing process eliminates singularities created during the recurrence phase of the surface's horizons, leading to a critical observation: a specific type of singularities cannot occur independently but must always appear in pairs. This fundamental property enables the classification of closed dilation surfaces, whose characterizing features reduce to a single essential property. Additionally, certain types of singularities cannot have multiple occurrences on a surface. This simplification reveals that a particular type of dilation surface is either empty or consists of a single point, demonstrating a contrasting behavior to general dilation surfaces, which can have multiple components.

Total association analysis is presented as a novel method for examining complex cognitive data without preconceived notions about specific cognitive elements. The approach relies on radial arithmetic to simplify the complex nature of brain connectivity and is applied to depth-of-processing event-related potentials, which confirms its ability to capture fine details of brain function with greater precision than existing methods. Furthermore, the methodology's adaptability is demonstrated through its ability to handle both temporal and spatial brain connectivity data with ease.

This study offers an in-depth exploration of the Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transformation (SBT) within the context of function spaces over $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and Euclidean space $L_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$, treating SBT either as a linear mapping between vector fields and functions or between polynomials and polynomials. By utilizing the Taylor isomorphism, which links the domains of polynomials in Clifford algebra and multivector polynomials, the paper extends the well-known applications of the SB transformation in positive operator-valued measures, functional calculus, quantum mechanics, and signal processing to the realm of multiquantum mechanics and multichannel signal processing. The text presents a comprehensive overview of SB transformation theory, including the generators of unitary groups, differential equations for evolution, and Taylor isomorphism theory, offering novel insights in this area.
