The computational expense of direct numerical simulations makes it difficult to utilize data from every parameter in multidimensional problems. Instead, statistical models can be utilized to approximate the problem's behavior. These models, often called surrogates, can be obtained through machine learning techniques such as those applied to Gaussian processes. Nevertheless, standard Gaussian process regression suffers from computational limitations in three or more dimensional spaces, where it becomes computationally costly to invert the dimensionality's covariance matrix. To overcome this, we suggest utilizing the reduced basis method with Gaussian process regression in one-dimensional cross sections to efficiently establish surrogate models for two-dimensional and three-dimensional problems. Furthermore, we derive the closure terms for the Taylor series expansion of the wind model, and apply these to accurately approximate the averaged Navier-Stokes equations. Additionally, we utilize the fast Fourier transform to efficiently calculate the surrogates, including its use in averaging the Navier-Stokes equations. These methods were successfully applied to simulate the load-bias characteristics of offshore wind turbines under realistic atmospheric conditions. The results reveal that incorporating the Navier-Stokes equations' Taylor series expansion and load-bias correlation terms significantly decreases the error. The incorporation of the Taylor series expansion resulted in a 65% reduction of the error when compared to using only the Navier-Stokes equations. The correlation terms provided an additional error reduction of 25%.

Following the severe earthquakes in Turkey that resulted in extensive loss of life and property destruction, particularly in the cities of Izmir, Sinop, and Karain, social media platforms such as Twitter became a pivotal channel for individuals to seek help and find each other during the disaster and in the aftermath. This research involves the examination of Twitter data related to the Izmir earthquake, which incorporates an exploratory data analysis. It combines statistical data analysis, thematic mapping, and sentiment analysis to create a comprehensive understanding of the impacts of the earthquakes. The data analysis revealed that people used Twitter to seek each other and request emergency aid. Additionally, the results show a negative sentiment in the data, indicating that individuals were emotionally distressed following the devastating earthquakes.
The $R_\infty$-character of a finite nilpotent group is fully determined, and a formula for finding it in the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups is also established.

A new approach is developed to identify the path of a solitary wave in a 1+1 dimensional medium over time, based solely on the wave's evolution. This path is represented by a series of unknown coordinates (x, y). An unknown function that describes Y in terms of X and time is used to frame the problem, with parameters (v0, c0, w0, b0) defining this description. Initially, V0 and W0 represent how fast the wave travels in the direction of the x-axis and its thickness, respectively. By approximating the electric field in a 1+1 dimensional medium using a hyperbolic tangent, this problem can be mapped to an optimization problem involving a constraint, with the goal of identifying the path of the wave. A successful implementation of this approach on simulated data yields highly accurate results, with limited requirements for initial conditions. Furthermore, this approach is applied to time-resolved data of fundamental solitons from experiments conducted at the Jefferson Lab, with the results being consistent with observed evidence. These new findings provide new insights into the fundamental mechanics of fundamental solitons, with the results being applicable to electron distribution as well.

Current advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles were primarily trained on controlled datasets that neglect the complexity of real-world driving situations. To better understand the behavior of these systems in everyday driving scenarios, it is crucial to develop a more comprehensive and situation-aware dataset. To address this need, we introduce SceNDD, a novel naturalistic driving dataset that categorizes and annotates a significant quantity of driving video data based on predefined traffic situations. Our annotated dataset includes over 500,000 instances of common urban driving scenarios, utilizing a hierarchical situation mapping framework. This framework is then utilized to evaluate multiple neural network models, all trained on the same set of situation-specific images extracted from the dataset. Our experiments reveal that models trained on situation-aware data outperform those trained on standard RGB images in terms of object detection accuracy across various driving scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate that a bottleneck compression method applied to our situation-specific dataset maintains the performance of the models without substantial compression, thus enabling the efficient transfer of large driving datasets to a more manageable size utilizing a situation-based framework. This research presents a groundbreaking dataset for the naturalistic driving community that addresses the gap between structure engineering and real-world driving behaviors. Furthermore, our methodology offers a replicable approach for developing and annotating large, situation-aware datasets from any naturalistic driving video.

In an interface CFT, the reflected entropy acts as a complementary counterpart to the entanglement Hamiltonian and mutual entropy, offering a way to quantify the level of correlation between two separate subsystems. For instance, in anisotropic scaling interfaces, the scalar precursor to the reflected entropy exhibits a specific proportional relationship with temperature and mutual entropy. Furthermore, various interfaces - such as those in holographic duals, gauge theories, and lattice models - have been found to display reflected entropy that grows linearly with logarithmic temperature, meets the monotonicity axiom, and conforms to a universal asymptotic slope in pure states. These findings support the idea that interfaces play a central role in understanding the properties of CFTs.

A reliable and efficient channel estimation algorithm for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface Assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing systems has been proposed, capable of handling incomplete channel data and inaccurate non-linearity in low-resolution Analog-to-Digital Converters within the receiver. To strengthen the estimation, additional techniques such as data supplementation, noise reduction, and low-frequency prediction are integrated, leading to enhanced performance. The proposed method outperforms conventional Enhanced Least Square solution, achieving betterestimation performance with reduced computational complexity compared to conventional methods like Monte-Carlo based non-linear least square solution and Bayesian least square solution. The evaluation of the proposed method demonstrates its ability to estimate Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface Assisted OFDM channels with low computational overhead and superior performance compared to conventional methods.

A robust fluctuation theorem applies to a broad class of non-equilibrium statistical systems, ensuring that specific properties remain preserved in their statistical thermodynamics. A crucial test has shown that system entropy, on average, does not decrease more rapidly than it increases. This same test can be employed to demonstrate the existence of a measurable, systematic, and irreversible thermodynamic potential for single energy systems. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that this potential is accessible through non-invasive observation of these systems. This potential, known as the Gibbs free energy, represents a fundamental thermodynamic property that differs significantly from entropy. Importantly, our findings not only validate the applicability of the integral fluctuation theorem to single energy systems but also provide new insights to understanding non-equilibrium systems and their behavior. This work lays the groundwork for future experimental projects, enabling the direct measurement of a thermodynamic potential for such systems.

We're exploring the deformations of G2instantons on nearly G2 manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between smooth deformations of a G2instanton and the space of self-dual connections on the associated tangent bundle that coincide with the original G2instanton when the deformation is zero. This linking, initially noticed by Karabegov for a Cauchy-Riemann operator on a nearly G2 manifold, is validated here in a more general context. This, in turn, allows us to separate the space of self-dual connections into two parts based on their association with G2instantons. We also examine how deformations of an L2 Dolbeault complex influence the associated instanton classes.

The coronavirus pandemic globally and its subsequent spread in numerous countries have resulted in the implementation of various measures, such as social isolation, to contain the outbreak. In an effort to curb the epidemic more effectively, many governments have introduced additional tools, including contact tracing programs, to identify individuals who have come into contact with infected persons. In line with this, several countries have developed and deployed mobile applications to enforce COVID-19 contact tracing measures, which collect users' location data and that of those with whom they have interacted. The aim of this work is to investigate the security risks associated with these contact tracing apps, which compromise users' location privacy. In response, a novel theoretical framework is presented to evaluate the confidentiality of these contact tracing apps, along with location privacy. The proposed approach, and its associated location privacy-based evaluation framework, are validated through simulations, and its relevance is also discussed via a real-world example involving Colombia, which has seen significant COVID-19 cases in recent years. The outcome of this research identifies and potentially informs future security measures to mitigate the inherent risks associated with these contact tracing apps.

The application of quantum processes to computational models is becoming increasingly prominent, with one area of focus being quantum neural networks. Theoretical frameworks for quantization are being developed to facilitate the transition of traditional deep learning models into the quantum domain. This work contrasts two distinct approaches for quantizing neural networks, emphasizing the importance of incorporating feedback loops to rectify errors and maintain accuracy. We demonstrate that applying quantum processes in isolation can compromise the overall learning process, ultimately disrupting the training data. The utilization of feedback mechanisms, on the other hand, permits the sustained generation of accurate data throughout the learning process. Furthermore, we explore potential applications for quantized neural networks, including enhanced data encryption methods.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

Two previously unidentified planetary bodies, which orbit within the 1:4 resonance zone of the Neptune's outer regions, have been hypothesized to be responsible for the orbital variances experienced by the 39991 Iochroma and its neighboring asteroids. Our study focuses on these hypothetical bodies and their potential dynamical influence on the surrounding asteroids as they interact with the 1:4 resonance zone. By assuming the masses of the disputed asteroids to be negligible, our analysis reveals that the two unidentified bodies' masses can be calculated based on the dynamic influences they exert on the orbital bodies. This results in a predicted mass value of approximately 3.2 x 10^22 grams for the first body and 1.9 x 10^22 grams for the second body, suggesting they are relatively small, cubic structures spanning a few hundred kilometers in diameter. Our simulations further indicate the disputed asteroids' orbital paths can be accurately reconstructed through the point mass theory's application, suggesting the existence of these hypothetical bodies is not necessary to explain the orbital variances in the 39991 Iochmona's group.

Building upon Ramanujan's earlier work on odd zeta values, we establish a formula using Hurwitz zeta functions, thereby providing a comprehensive and alternative expression for the inverse of the Riemann zeta function at odd integers. We present a direct verification of a previously proposed generalization by Beukers, as well as an intuitive, straightforward approach to Ramanujan's original result. Furthermore, by extending one of Bachmann's equations for the Hurwitz zeta function, we establish a novel relationship involving the product of two such functions, ultimately ultimately leading to an alternate derivation of the original formula originally discovered by Ramanujan. The approach presented gains additional significance due to its simplicity and the derivation of a novel, useful identity for products of Hurwitz zeta functions.

We investigate a complex generalizing extended elliptic cohomology theories, 
infiming a crucial role for CP(V) in this context. Specifically, for a given 
finite field F, we construct a cohomology theory, denoted E, with properties 
equivalent to F[1]-equivariant cohomology of CP(V) and also satisfying a 
logical circle equivariance. In addition, we prove E is isomorphic to a modified 
version of complex elliptic cohomology, specifically the reduction of the complex 
version to the finite field F.

Recent applications of algebraic topology in physics have been gaining momentum, with homotopy theory and mapping cone methods emerging as key tools. By combining these techniques with machine learning, researchers can address some of the most pressing challenges in the field. For example, transforming complex continuous equations into trainable neural network models has made various physical problems more tractable. We demonstrate this process for a simplified Navier-Stokes problem and explore the corresponding stable states.

This study provides detailed, next-to-leading-order calculations for certain $J/\psi$ observables produced in conjunction with light quark flavors, along with comparisons to existing data from the BESII experiment at Beijing. Specifically, the calculations investigate angular anisotropy measurements from the decay of $J/\psi$ to $l^+ l^-$, along with transverse momentum distributions for $J/\psi$. Notably, both $\eta_c$ and combined $\chi_{cJ}$ contributions are included in the calculations.

Our study gathered online feedback from 1,005 Signal app users, including 469 who were active in the past week, to compare their perceptions of app-specific PINs to third-party PINs. The results showed that 55% of users found the Signal PINs clear, while 21% didn't understand them. When users were asked to identify the Signal PINs' purposes, 75% failed to answer correctly, with 35% stating they had no idea. The most understood Signal PIN was the encryption indicator, but even so, 35% of users were unsure. Interestingly, users were more likely to understand Signal PINs that provided apparent goals, like verifying age or location requirements, than those that served unique purposes, such as detecting country or pseudonymity.

This application paper accompanies a preprint: "Efficient numerical integration of the solar spectrum" (arXiv:2101.0782). We demonstrate the utility of the solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature rule for calculating the integral of the solar energy spectrum. This rule offers the advantage of guaranteed precision, provided the number of points in the integration is sufficiently high. The underlying theory from of the spectral theory of quadrature formulas ensures this precision. We show the solar energy spectrum can be accurately approximated within an error of less than $10^{-5}$ using just 41 points. This enables the efficient calculation of the overall solar energy flux at a point on Earth, taking into account atmospheric filter effects. This efficient calculation can be applied in various solar energy applications without relying on the widely used DISRTEM solar energy model.

The second-order curvature information of a function is its Hessian matrix. Due to the substantial computational expense of calculating the Hessian, scientists employ the generalized Gauss-Newton's diminished structure (ggnd) as a more efficient alternative for approximating its curvature. The ggnd's structure comprises a Hessian-like matrix that can evaluate the inner product of vectors and determine their dimensionality with $O(N^2)$ complexity, making it suitable for large-scale nonlinear least-squares problems. The diminished structure's outer product can be further utilized to calculate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Hessian approximation. The presented method, viViT, utilizes these properties, allowing for a procedure for accurately identifying the stationary points and local directions of nonlinear, highly-constrained optimization problems with discriminant analysis and least-squares minimization as test cases.

Beis-Dart et al.'s findings (2020) suggest that in languages specifying grammatical gender for nouns, people more frequently associate male nouns with animate objects and female nouns with inanimate objects. This study confirms the phenomenon and explores its connection with how grammatical gender affects noun representations. To do this, the research uses German as a case study, German being an example of a language specifying grammatical gender for nouns that also expresses part-of-speech and gender categorization. By analyzing it through the lens of word embeddings, the study found that in German, grammatical gender influences noun representations to distinguish between male and female entities more significantly than in English, with the distinction being particularly evident in animate objects. This study further shows that these biases are more pronounced in contexts where the grammatical gender of objects is known. These results support the idea that people utilize conceptual linkages between linguistic categories and other language elements to establish associations between grammatical gender and part-of-speech. This study's discovery of a connection between grammatical gender and part-of-speech categorization highlights how using word embeddings from natural language models can provide insight into the nature of these categorizations.

In this paper, we develop the concept of charmability for certain discrete groups acting on hyperbolic spaces, and show that the charmability of these groups is closely linked to their rigidity properties. Specifically, we demonstrate that the charmability of a discrete group G implies its rigidity, and this phenomenon occurs not only in HEE sets but also in more general contexts such as foliated spaces and CW-complexs. Notably, our results provide an alternative proof of the rigidity of arithmetic groups that are based on simple algebras.

Estimating the pose of an object provides crucial spatial information essential for numerous AI applications. The typical approach to the pairwise estimation of rotation and translation angles in millimeter accuracy is cumbersome and complicated by rotation ambiguity and lack of calibration equipment. The problem is further exacerbated by objects with multiple parts that can be positioned arbitrarily. The proposed solution is an innovative method for training a neural network that can determine a class-specific coordinate frame without any specific training on the object for which the pose needs to be estimated. The network is trained with 1000 object classes from the MS-COCO dataset, and our results indicate that zero-shot class-level pose estimation with our technique outperforms both sample-level estimation and class-level estimation using PCL libraries in all scenarios. Moreover, our method compares favorably to recent techniques reported in the field. The source code for estimating object pose is available at https://github.com/HsuingNgaimi2/Zero-shot-Object-Pose.

Traffic forecasting plays a significant role in optimizing transportation systems, with many current systems facing critical limitations. Existing sparse traffic prediction models typically rely on comprehensive data from training periods, but this is impractical due to associated high data costs and the risk of model inaccuracies resulting from training on incomplete data. In response, this study proposes a novel, efficient framework for sparse traffic prediction by training an autoencoder with sparse data, using similarity-based targeting techniques to improve prediction accuracy. The framework integrates dual targeting strategies: one standard approach using comprehensive data, and another based on similarity that integrates additional contextual information to produce more accurate predictions. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on real-world data from multiple cities.

This study presents VACA, a model that utilizes causal concepts to address interfering factors and capture crucial interactions in observational data, applying these insights to predict outcomes under different scenarios. By incorporating the causal minimality principle, researchers developed a comprehensive model that encompasses various types of causal relationships. Building on this, a causal representation learning framework was established to identify key factors contributing to the model. Experimental results demonstrate that VACA efficiently handles interference and captures interdependent relationships better than existing variants of graph neural networks and other comparison models. Furthermore, VACA effectively addresses complex questions about hypothetical situations, offering a potential solution in areas such as healthcare.

The upcoming decade is expected to be an exciting one for Fast Radio Burst (FRB) research, thanks to a significant surge in data volumes from next-generation radio telescopes. These increased capabilities will necessitate high-speed processing and detection algorithms. Our network, REALTA, is designed to collect FRB-like transient data from multiple telescopes and facilitate real-time analysis by engaging the community in shaping the pipeline's design. Here, we outline the initial findings of REALTA during its testing phase at the Irish LOFAR station, focusing on particular sorries stemming from hardware issues and data processing. Our analysis encompasses a thorough examination of system performance, including source speed limitations due to the absence of antenna mode data, detection rates in REALTA, and the detection efficiency of current FRB catalog entries. Additionally, we investigate the effectiveness of various detection methods, including sliding spectrogram and filter bank, and the optimal duration for the former. Our findings imply that the optimal detection strategy depends on data sample rates, while the optimal duration for the sliding spectrogram method is influenced by the number of frequency channels.

We create an advanced form of metasystems using "clever" metaphotonics by leveraging artificial intelligence and machine learning tools. Initially, we refine design criteria for metasystems that manipulate light quickly by using data from ferromagnetic surface waves. Next, we employ neural networks to improve our understanding of light behavior in complex structures. Our analysis in 2D metasystems shows that specific patterns, like high symmetry or order, are crucial for maintaining light's unique properties. Our simulation results also demonstrate that these metasystems can control light with a wide range of frequencies in both traditional and magnetic materials. Our exploration of 3D metasystems shows that similar principles apply, and we predict that these metasystems could lead to new types of magnetic phenomena that have never been seen before. Our research utilizes machine learning to predict how different structure changes affect physical properties, which could lead to breakthroughs in topological physics and for discovering new materials. Our findings represent an important development in the study of light and matter, and could soon lead to innovative technologies that manipulate light quickly and efficiently.

Our goal is to analyze how characteristics influencing film success before release
affect actual revenue. To this end, we've developed a film dataset with 2,185 films
spanning 15 years, along with 5 key attributes. This film dataset will facilitate
further research into how film characteristics impact revenue, an area that has seen
significant previous investigation. Utilizing our newly acquired data, we employed
bivariate correlation analysis to examine the relationships between the five film
attributes and revenue, and subsequently examined subgroups to verify if these
correlations hold within more specific groupings. Notably, our findings reveal that
as film duration increases so does revenue, whereas more elaborate films actual
ize lower revenue, and an inconsistent relationship was discovered between film
rating and revenue across different film groupings. Conversely, the number of acting
 stars present in films has no discernable effect on revenue as established through
the analysis of both the overall film population and a subset division of the film
collection.

This study explores the role of auxiliary frequency regulation in managing voltage instability in power grids. A study using the IEEE 30-bus system revealed that frequency stability might be compromised even in scenarios with low-nuclear penetration, prompting the investigation of auxiliary frequency regulation (AFR). A theoretical framework for analyzing small signal stability in power grids is developed and applied to contexts with and without AFR. Additionally, the research examines both linear and nonlinear stability and simulates dynamic behavior using time-domain simulations. The findings indicate that AFR enhances both voltage stability and power grid performance, consistent with numerical results from the case study.

Cyber Physical Systems networks require high-performance and intelligent management in managing network-flows, transference of data and resource allocation decisions. The implementation of such tasks in different networks calls for various strategies of resource allocation, specifically for bandwidth, storage, and data center capacities. Existing solutions, like distributed algorithms based on complementarity, utilize local information for making global decisions. However, some decisions may not meet system optimality, such as energy efficiency or total performance. In this work, we propose a new performance optimization method that takes into account the intricate dynamics present in networks of networks and multi-resource management. The proposed solution takes into account non-linear energy consumption, capacity limitations, processing speed, and communication latency in networks. The work presents an analytical model using Matrices, Non-linear Control Theory, and Optimization Techniques. The solution was tested and validated using simulations on complex networks, such as cloud-based networks, Resource pool networks, and IoT networks. The results show a significant performance improvement, specifically up to 100% in performance compared to current approaches.

In a previous study, the Monte-Carlo model MAPPIES was developed to simulate non-thermal Compton scattering of partially polarized UV photons by relativistic electrons in the vicinity of compact objects. This paper presents an application of the MAPPIES model to modeling blazar spectra, specifically the continuum radiation. The model includes two mechanisms: a thermal electron component reminiscent of the Standard Model, and a non-thermal electron component producing a distinctive "bump' in the spectrum at short wavelengths. Together, these two components explain the 'u-shaped' spectrum observed in certain blazars below 1000 eV as a superposition of a blackbody and a non-thermal continuum. The red wing of the Blazar UV/soft X-ray excess is produced by a relativistic electron beam Compton scattering polarized thermal photons, resulting in a characteristic hard X-ray spectrum. The model also reproduces the 'double-humped' optical to X-ray spectrum of BL Lacertae objects with the assistance of absorption and reflection effects typically present in these objects. Additionally, the MAPPIES model explains the 'excess' in the X-ray spectrum of Active Galaxies with a thermal component originating from their accretion disks and the mechanical perturbation of these disks by the accretion radius.

A general method is developed to create extended objects by shifting its local components when projected onto complex surfaces. This approach can seamlessly translate local data with varying dimensions, domains, or formats into a uniform grid of points, allowing for a unified framework to apply spatial transformations. This formulation is based on a polynomial mixture of spatial interpolation techniques, including natural neighbor, bilinear/bicubic, and radial basis function methods. By combining these techniques, the method achieves high accuracy, including: the ability to handle diverse point clouds with complex geometries; preserving local properties such as tangency, orthogonality, and continuity; and maintaining consistent discretization. This formulation is also adaptable to various types of data, including scalar, vector, and tensor values. A key implementation detail is that the mapping is self-contained and does not require input from the original domain, making it highly versatile. Several case studies are provided to demonstrate the method's effectiveness in a variety of applications, including meshing complex surfaces, extending local mesh structures, and applying spatial mappings to multiple types of data.

In our study, we examined quantum measurements of two-particle systems in
symmetric states. Specifically, we investigated how various types of input states
are distinguished through measurements made on an identical pair, versus on a system
with its particle identities exposed. Notably, for states of known symmetry, no
better accuracy was achieved when comparing the results to their actual values. 
Conversely, for all asymmetric states, optimal accuracy was achieved. These 
findings led us to suggest a strategy for identifying unknown asymmetric states 
by first measuring local systems and then comparing shared attributes after the 
identification process.

Baryons are generated through a fragmentation process of a QCD fiber with properties inherited from the baryon itself. A specific phase of this fiber, characterized by its helical structure, naturally produces one baryon per fragmentation process, while the process is quantized. A detailed understanding of the fragment's tree structure, inherited from the original QCD field, is essential for accurate baryon formation. In addition, the new baryon's wave function is created through a combination of the old baryon's wave function and the interaction between the fragment and the associated quark/antiquark pairs. An essential aspect of this process involves the configuration of these quark/antiquark pairs, which can be described by a specific property of the fiber. Moreover, the process reveals a novel relationship between the fragment and these quark/antiquark pairs, which can be understood by considering the quantum translation of the original QCD field.

The main objective of studying solar helioseismically is to identify internal movements, using travel times of wave pulses reflected back from the sun's surface, to map its circulation patterns. However, the accuracy of these travel-time measurements is limited by irregularities in the data due to turbulent areas and other disturbances. To assess the potential of related movements in the data, we have developed a method to focus on the information generated near the active regions. This has a significant effect, particularly in the study of meridional circulation in the data, with a focus on the north-south flow in the data. Our analysis reveals a notable contribution from the data's movements in the regions around the active regions, which significantly affects travel-time measurements. This has particular implications for the study of solar rotation in the data and our understanding of meridional circulation in the data. This has significant consequences for the study of solar internal rotation and meridional circulation in the data.

Our research delves into the gravitational waves produced by massive cosmic structures forming within local electric fields that vary over time and have relatively short lifespans, as predicted by the post-inflationary landscape of our universe. These gravitational waves will eventually transform into an electromagnetic signal when they encounter the matter within these structures, a phenomenon termed "magnetic turbulence." Analyzing the gravitational waves emitted by a network of pulsars, and contrasting their predicted behavior with existing pulsar timing array data, presents us with two possible outcomes based on the power spectrum of the primordial magnetic field, often described using the $\alpha$ parameter. If the primordial magnetic field is of a high-frequency type, as indicated by an $\alpha$ parameter value greater than three, the gravitational waves emitted will be too weak to be detected through the pulsar timing array data. On the other hand, if the $\alpha$ parameter is lower than three, the gravitational waves emitted will be strong enough to be detected, a situation that we can further investigate by analyzing the differences between the predicted gravitational signal and the observed data.

Light field technology is highly sought-after for next-generation displays, with image compression as a top priority. While existing methodologies fail to meet practical standards, our innovative approach combines cutting-edge learning techniques with expert input to create a more realistic image model. By incorporating expert knowledge into a traditional Continuous Image Synthesis Neural Network, our method significantly reduces compression time and achieves higher quality results. Our model considers the relationship between adjacent pixels in different viewing angles as being driven by distinct factors such as light source, material, environment, and optical effects. A new neural architecture is introduced, Disparity-Conscious 3D Knotted Network (DCKN), to capture these effects and minimize the impact of each other's interference. Our expertise also influences the way images are broken down and compressed. As a result, our DCKN-based approach far exceeds current state-of-the-art solutions in terms of compression ratio and qualitative image restoration capabilities.

A key challenge in cross-lingual information retrieval is effectively translating queries and documents into a common language, despite differences in their linguistic structures. This study investigates the potential benefits of merging interactive and non-interactive frameworks in vector-based crosslingual retrieval. To achieve this, a novel approach called Trans4clicer is introduced, designed to improve crosslingual retrieval by aligning query and document vectors with mutual attention. The experiments conducted on a large dataset demonstrate that the combination of these two frameworks, utilizing the Ensemble4clicer method, yields superior results in terms of average precision and map@3, outperforming current state-of-the-art models, including LexRank and MULE.

Several developing nations, including Indonesia, face significant challenges related to spatial health disparities and limited access to high-quality healthcare, highlighting the need for effective small-area estimation. This issue is particularly prominent in low and middle-income countries, which often struggle with inadequate healthcare infrastructure and resource constraints. In response, many of these countries have intensified the use of geographic information systems combined with electronic health records, thereby leveraging the potential for spatial analytics based on predictive machine learning algorithms in the enhancement of healthcare services. This study investigates the comparative performance of various estimation techniques, including empirical Bayesian, synthetic, and block bootstrap methods. A district-level healthcare dataset in Indonesia serves as the basis for our exploratory empirical analysis. Through simulated real-world scenarios, we examine the limitations of synthetic and block bootstrap estimators when applied to low and middle-income nations. Ultimately, we provide recommendations for the selection of suitable estimators in the context of these countries, emphasizing the importance of theoretical calculations of various biases and variances as a critical design consideration.

The classical Kelly betting strategy is an optimal method for individuals who can place repeated bets with a bookmaker, providing a guaranteed, long-term profit. When dealing with a system that offers multiple possible outcomes, the quantum Kelly betting approach has been developed to provide the best possible returns for repeated bets with a bookmaker, outperforming the classic method in certain high-entropy scenarios. To improve performance in scenarios with low entropy, a new betting strategy based on a continuous variable model is proposed, using a quantum memory. By treating each bet as a quantum state that evolves after each update, the betting problem can be resolved through the calculation of the optimal density matrix for each update, ensuring that the density matrix remains positive definite. A simulation of the strategy is also provided, demonstrating its performance in various real-world sports betting scenarios. By employing the covariance matrix representation of the density matrix, the risk associated with this low-entropy scenario with quantum memory can be compared to the risk in high-entropy scenarios with the classic or quantum Kelly approaches.

Compound semiconductors with the general formula MA$_2$Z$_4$ (where M is Mo, W, or Ti, and A is Si or Ge) have drawn attention for their potential in highly performing semiconductor materials. Using advanced computational methods, including ab initio calculations and density functional theory, we analyzed the electronic structure and band arrangement of these materials. The study reveals that Mo, Wi, and Ti have identical energetic preferences for Si and Ge, as well as identical energetic preferences for N, P, and As. Furthermore, it appears that the stacking order of these materials does not affect their band gap order or the arrangement of energy levels. The findings suggest that the band gap order remains consistent due to the balanced density of states at the conduction band edge, whereas the arrangement of energy levels is attributed to the identical ordering of orbital components in this energy range. Consequently, it is the excitons, rather than the band structures, whose stacking-order-dependent properties require thorough examination for applications in MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds.

A note on my previous response:  The calculation of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ matrix element using QCD instantons is based on the approach developed by Geng and Salek, and its application to the $\Sigma^+ \to p$ transition is straightforward.  The resulting estimate, when considering the influence of the charm quark mass effect, yields a value for the branching ratio of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ process at approximately $4.2 \times 10^{-12}$.  This outcome appears to contradict the LHCb experiment's inability to detect such a rare transition, with an observed upper limit of $3.8 \times 10^{-12}$ at a $95\%$ confidence level.

Using complex simulations, we explore how a protoplanetary disk is formed from the transformation of a pre-stellar core. Through multiple phases, starting with radiative cooling and eventually switching to non-radiative conditions, we observe the core collapse. The protoplanetary disk emerges when a cloud of gas ceases to be gravitationally bound. An additional set of simulations, incorporating realistic rates of chemical reactions, reveals how the core's composition evolves over time. According to our simulations, the core's temperature is nearly constant during the initial collapse, but drops significantly with the adoption of non-radiative conditions. This results in the disk retaining warm outer layers and creating thermal gradients within it. An observed phenomenon known as 'filamentary structure' can be attributed to the core's inner layer cooling at a faster rate than its outer layers. Furthermore, our simulations suggest that the core's inner layers are enriched with carbon and oxygen through chemical reactions. When the disk forms, this results in the outer layers being predominantly composed of hydrogen and helium, while the inner layers contain carbon and oxygen. An additional set of simulations, which utilized non-radiative conditions, revealed the formation of a chemically stratified disk. According to our analysis, this disk will undergo dynamic changes as it evolves over time, ultimately giving rise to a star with a consistent metal-to-hydrogen ratio and low initial mass.

Incorporating the knowledge of atmospheric disturbances generated by wind into standard atmospheric refraction models yields an essential improvement in recovering the source of light emitted by celestial objects observed from the ground. Following our 2021 study, which used the Hake camera to detect tip-tilt scintillation signals, this research presents a detailed examination of these atmospheric disturbances, specifically the correlations between wind speed and irregularity. By combining our previous measurements with the ROPARO satellite's scintometry data, we studied the characteristics of wind speed and its relationship with irregularity, including their impacts on diffraction limits, image stability, and the estimation of flux losses due to atmospheric disturbances. This research enabled us to establish a probabilistic model of irregularity as it varies with altitude, leading to an expansion of the diffraction limit equation to incorporate the effects of wind speed and irregularity. Moreover, our analysis reveals that, on average, the movement of irregularities generates the dominant contribution to the scaling of their transverse correlations, exceeding the effects of their rotational movement.

We have introduced a novel temporal-decision-making model, the multi-period dependency model, which captures the sparsity-dependent relationships within sequences of data over multiple time periods. Traditional time series models, such as AR/GARCH/EEG, focus on either sparse relationships within short intervals or multiple periods but lack a unified framework. Our proposed model utilizes a Bayesian approach with a multinomial probability distribution and the stick-breaking process to describe dependency patterns, thereby generating dependencies within sequences of data based on sparse draws. To accommodate varying dependency periods, we integrated the hierarchical Dirichlet process to enable the model to learn dependency periods and their respective parameters. Our model, being a hidden state model, relies on the EM algorithm for parameter estimation and model sampling, which allows us to provide uncertainty metrics. Simulation results using synthetic data as well as real-world data on daily COVID-19 cases in the US demonstrate the model's capability to identify patterns, including frequent patterns, infrequent patterns, and unique events such as the 2020 COVID-19 surge in the US.

This brief comment links two distinct areas of study: the realm of abelian groups and the world of non-classical propositional logics. Specifically, the connection is established between the dual theory of groups topologically similar to the groups used in abelian group theory and the'stability' property found in free distributive lattices, as well as its equivalent'staunchness' property in distributive lattices. A well-known result by Bonnay et al. reveals an exact correspondence between the stable and distributive lattices, which is further generalized here. Moreover, the established relationship between the dual theory of groups and the'stability' property provides valuable insights into the structure of distributive lattices and their potential applications in propositional logic, leading to the conclusion that the exponents of artinian robustly stable lattices have specific properties and can be represented as $2$-groups.

The rapid advancement of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has resulted in an explosive generation of data, prompting a shift towards utilizing machine learning for IoT hierarchy construction, especially in building intelligent cities. However, conventional machine learning methods often struggle with geographic, economic, and cultural constraints on data accessibility, making decentralized or edge computing on IoT devices increasingly vital. As such, federated learning emerges as a promising solution, bringing benefits of enhanced data security, increased data utilization, improved privacy, and reduced communication overhead. Nevertheless, the implementation of federated learning still poses significant challenges in terms of equity, particularly in developing regions, thus highlighting the need for further research. Furthermore, the existing federated learning frameworks frequently overlook differential privacy, which poses a significant risk to clients' privacy, thus necessitating rigorous differential privacy protocols for secure machine learning on IoT platforms. In response to these pressing concerns, the study introduces a novel framework that leverages federated learning for developing intelligent cities, emphasizing equity and differential privacy considerations.

A proposed model is the Supersymmetric Minimal U(1) X model, which introduces a novel nature of dark matter alongside the concept of dark charge. This model has the potential to meet all experimental requirements for dark matter and cosmic rays. The research shows that dark matter in this model consists of a simple composition of supersymmetric particles, with the dark matter particle being a bosonic or fermionic lepton under U(1) X. With a minimal supersymmetric model where superparticles appear at the TeV scale, this model is consistent with baryon number long-lived particle observations from LHC experiments. The study presents the model's complete particle spectrum and coupling constants, which appear at the renormalable Standard Model gauge levels. The research focuses on dark matter density in the Universe, which is shown to be consistent with the observed present day cosmic dark matter density, based on data from cosmic density surveys such as Planck, LAMOST and DDRLF4. Additionally, this model is tested against various experimental findings, which show that supersymmetric particles, predicted by the model, have masses in the range of a few TeV and below and are beyond the detection capacity of current LHC experiments. The research indicates that this model is capable of producing testable predictions, which can be examined through upcoming data from LHC and JHEP, as well as potential signatures from dark matter annihilation in cosmic rays observed with the Alpha-GAMMA and AMEGO experiments.

Our research focuses on designing an IRS-aided wireless-powered network that is capable of withstanding interference. In this setup, the IRS is used to direct the energy-harvesting receiver's direct signal from the transmitter, while the remaining energy-harvesting receiver is obstructed by the IRS. Initially, we formulate an optimization problem to enhance the receiver's energy harvesting under interference by adjusting the IRS's reflection matrix. However, this optimization proves to be a solvable but complex problem due to its high dimensionality and non-linearity. In order to avoid computational challenges associated with this optimization, we develop an unsupervised learning-based alternative approach. Here, the IRS's optimal configuration is encoded on a compact embedding vector and an associated associative memory network called "E2EM". This E2EM is trained such that when given the input of the interference pattern, corresponding to the energy harvesting receiver blocked by the IRS, it outputs the optimal IRS configuration to maximise the energy harvesting by the receiving device. We validate our "E2EM" method, demonstrating its substantial performance gain over the conventional tuning method that uses a solver. Moreover, we reveal that "E2EM" closely approximates the performance of a comprehensive and solvable but computationally intractable convex optimization method.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Tl. The measurement was conducted at the University of Edinburgh's Tandem-10 accelerator facility around 183 days before the $^{186}$Hg peak decays. The study provided the mass difference between parent and daughter nuclei as -14.711(27) MeV, thereby supplementing and validating earlier theoretical calculations. Moreover, it discovered 84.8(30) percent of the initial $^{186}$Hg decay strength, assigning this to the 1053 keV state in $^{186}$Tl, a finding that contrasts with theoretical predictions of a mixed Gamow-Teller nature with a significant mix of the intruder $i_{1/2}$ proton configuration.

We have explored the potential link between the cosmological dark energy and leptogenesis in a unified framework based on an SO(10)-inspired supersymmetric model with a high-scale seesaw mechanism. The dark energy sector is introduced through a couple of hidden sector fields forming a non-negative, time-varying dark energy density. The universal scalar field's dynamics influences both the dark energy density and the quintessence dynamics. Additionally, we have examined how the dark energy density relates to the neutrino mass matrix's eigenvalue close to zero, generating small neutrino masses. Depending on this eigenvalue's sign, we have found two options for coupling strength between the dark sector and right-handed neutrinos, either directly or indirectly. With hierarchical light neutrino masses, we have determined that their masses are in the range of 0.4-0.6 meV. Given the model's archetypal nature, we have made meV-level predictions rather than exactly solvable values to account for the neutrino mass scale's inherent uncertainty. With electronvolts-level leptonphobic couplings to the dark sector, we have found that the associated mass generated during leptogenesis is below the observable range, making it only a theoretically viable option. This theoretical perspective on leptogenesis becomes applicable if future observational data verify the existence of neutrino masses in the meV range.

Many control problems involve tasks that require robots to execute specific motions in order to accomplish tasks like reaching, walking, or flying. Current data-driven approaches to control often struggle when dealing with limited information on a particular task, yet they have access to a wealth of unrelated data and expertise. To address this issue, a new method is presented that takes advantage of side information as well as unrelated data. It does this by using a novel algorithm to find the most effective control strategies for a variety of tasks, one of which may be entirely new, all based on just one trial each. The method also includes tools such as a new feature engineering technique and a simulator, that make it easier to identify the most effective control strategies. It is shown that using side information and unrelated data together leads to better results, in fact substantially so, in a simulated air-assembly control scenario. Additionally, the method's performance is compared to existing approaches in a number of real-world control challenges and it is found to work effectively in all the cases it was tested with.

All Toda conformal field models possess a hidden integrable structure which is based on the affine Lie algebra $A_{2n-1}^{(2)}$. When the model is characterized by a value of $n$ equal to 3, an analogy to the integrable systems developed by Deconinck, Hydon, and Ramond emerges, and this correspondence reveals a set of equations known as Ward identities which are closely related to the affine Lie algebra $A_{2n-1}^{(2)}$. Specifically, when the value of $n$ is 3, a set of four equations known as Ward identities can be derived, and these equations can be matched to the systems studied by Deconinck, Hydon, and Ramond. Furthermore, the Toda conformal field model exhibits a dual structure which is analogous to an integrable system defined by the Kashiwara--Toda equation in the context of the $A_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ Lie algebra.

Despite significant advancements in generating realistic images, previous top-performing GAN architectures, such as FPN and RelNets, have not been thoroughly examined. This study proposes a novel GAN architecture that integrates FN with a triplet loss in disentanglement (RTLD) to achieve a better understanding of the interplay between FN and GAN. FN with triplet loss produces superior results on four datasets, surpassing other top-performing methods, with a notable improvement of 2.5% in FID score on the LSUN church dataset. Furthermore, this study provides evidence of better training stability in FN-based GANs, lower mode collapse, and higher diversity in samples generated from the proposed RTLD architecture, suggesting that incorporating relation networks in GANs is a valuable approach.

We have successfully implemented dual-field quantum key distribution (QKD) without phase modulation requirements, achieving this within an unsupervised environment. Our protocol utilizes two distinct field states generated by beam splitters in conjunction with quantum key distribution based on intensity, thereby circumventing the need for precise phase control. A previously developed approach enabled the conversion of magnetic storage device disk patterns into the necessary dual-field states. Our test platform, consisting of single-mode fibers and combined power splitters within a hybrid setup, served to enhance security through an integrated efficient rapid random QKD system. A total of $8,000$ bits per second key generation rate was achieved, along with $1.68$ bit per photon efficiency. This breakthrough allows the secure exchange of information between large numbers of parties.

In this research, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of certain weighted shift operators on the Hilbert space l^2(<u>ℵ</u>) and the Bergman space A^2_α, specifically examining the necessary and sufficient conditions that need to be imposed on the weighting function, σ, in order for these algebras to be linearly embedded within the Cohn algebra. Previous studies, such as the work by Bonilla-Muñoz and Potts, have focused primarily on the case of the Hilbert space, and it has been shown that a necessary condition is that the function (1 + |ζ|)^-2σ(ζ) must be bounded above for |ζ| > 1. Conversely, for the Bergman space A^2_α, a necessary condition is that the function (1 + |ζ|)^-2σ(ζ) must be bounded above for |ζ| > 1 and the function (1 + |ζ|)^-ασ(ζ) must be bounded below for |ζ| > 1. Additionally, specific weighting functions, such as those involving polynomial functions, have been considered in the literature.

In order to enhance the accuracy of object detection algorithms, researchers have been focusing on the importance of annotation quality, particularly for tasks involving unfamiliar object categories. This study presents a novel solution to improve object detection in unfamiliar scenarios by utilizing pseudo annotations derived from lexical data. By applying this approach, researchers achieved superior results on the COCO text challenge with significant speed-ups in annotation creation, outperforming existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency. This achievement is attributed to pseudo annotation generation methods that utilize lexical data to produce high-quality annotation sets. Additionally, researchers analyzed the efficacy of combining two distinct text-based methods in alternating annotation generations, finding that alternating the annotation generation method led to greater diversity in the resulting annotations and improved overall performance.

The Rho Ophiuchus cloud, a prominent dark cloud located in Vela X-C, is readily visible and is primarily influenced by the nearby T Tauri star S1. Researchers conducted a study using the Australia Telescope Compact Array to observe Rho Ophiuchus at specific wavelengths while taking into consideration the contamination from nearby early-type stars. They discovered ionized gas and a large-scale outflow in the eastern region and, interestingly, two distinct emission pathways in the western region that could be attributed to either an outflow or multiple emission sources. Using the Atacama Large Array Observatory, scientists obtained spectral data of S1 which showed strong emission from ionized gas, and weaker signals from atomic and photoinduced molecular gas. They found an approximately 500 AU correlation radius between the ionized gas and the star S1, and a 1000 AU correlation radius with the atomic gas, which seemed to be consistent with the star's luminosity and radiative influence. The star S1 appears to be surrounded by a 100 AU corona, as deduced from the star's radiative influence and the detected emission. The star S1 has a mass similar to that of the T Tauri star TMC 148, which is part of the Taurus-Auriga molecular cloud.
