In the last decade, deep learning models have been employed successfully in various computer vision applications. The typical convolutional neural network (CNN) was the primary choice for computer vision tasks. A relatively new advancement is the transformer architecture, designed primarily for natural language processing. The ability of transformers to manage long-range data dependencies has made them attractive to the computer vision community. This paper provides an overview of using transformers in computer vision, covering their applications, combinations with CNNs, and distinctive components, including multi-head self-attention. We also explore recent works, focusing on their architecture and underlying techniques. This review aims to summarize recent research and identify promising areas for further study.

The purpose of this paper is to offer an interpretation of factor models that can address the criticism of lacking a theoretical underpinning. According to our argument, the process of predicting future outcomes involves reducing complex data and embedding this reduced information in a higher-dimensional space. By utilizing various techniques such as principal component analysis or independent component analysis, this enables the representation of data in a more simplified form. Furthermore, our approach utilizes a multi-class classifier like the Gaussian mixture model to project this reduced form onto class boundaries, effectively mapping to different probability distributions. It is demonstrated that this probabilistic mapping can be utilized for forecasting purposes. Specifically, it is shown that this method can be viewed as a dynamic model with time-variant connections between dimensions, where loadings for a unit are assumed to remain constant over time. Moreover, our results indicate the effectiveness of this framework in mortality forecasting, revealing accuracy at the individual level and aligning with macro-level trends.

When utilizing similar neural architectures in Random Search or Grid Search for model optimization, performance inconsistencies due to sampling and mixing architectures may undermine the effectiveness of these methods. To explore this issue, researchers discovered that a significant factor contributing to performance variability stems from interference between sampled or mixed architectures, which causes fluctuations in gradient magnitudes and network feature distributions. Based on these findings, a novel approach, called Clean Search, was developed to eliminate interference and thus boost the effectiveness of Random Search and NAS. Researchers compared Clean Search with Random Search and NAS in four diverse datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-32, and EMNIST-J, and resulted in an improvement in accuracy by up to 2.5% on all tested datasets. The source code for Clean Search has been made available online.

Time series data analysis is a crucial component of various scientific disciplines, encompassing fields such as finance, meteorology, and sports. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for attribute-based time series analysis and offers an innovative R package, theft, tailored to meet this objective. The R package's core functions facilitate data visualization, feature extraction, and behavior modeling, which can be applied independently or in conjunction with one another. The R package's performance is exemplified through an actual data set analysis, specifically the airpassenger data. This supplemental package to the ts features R functionality provides additional capabilities for time series attribute-based examination.

In this paper, we examine the boundary at infinity of complete CAT(0) spaces. We demonstrate that in contexts where boundary points have well-defined representations using geodesic rays, the space's convexity can be characterized based on the non-divergence of such rays. This notion is further clarified through the identification of conditions under which geodesic complete spaces have well-defined boundary points. We also explore examples and applications within the contexts of simplicial complexes and Cayley complexes.

Measuring translators' reliability is a crucial process that translates into evaluating the dependability of translated products such as software, documents, and devices. Translators with high reliability produce documentation that is less likely to contain errors. translators are individuals who convert written text from one language to another, whereas translation agents utilize tools such as machines or human translators to carry out the translation process. This study aims to develop a novel approach for assessing the dependability of translators by utilizing Bayesian Estimation of Discretionary Data (BEED) model. The proposed method involves calculating each translator's average rate of errors per unit of translated text and the variation in their performance. The methodology also accounts for potential biases common to all translators and those unique to individual translators. The effectiveness of the proposed method was evaluated through simulated research scenarios with adjusted translation performance.

We derive three key formulas that establish the total amount of energy that must be absorbed by an object to facilitate scattering. These rules apply to all situations: (i) when energy is absorbed uniformly, (ii) when energy is emitted into specific areas, and (iii) when energy is funneled through specific channels. Our findings are based on two fundamental principles: the definition of eigenchannels and two fundamental rules for energy conservation. We utilize this theoretical framework to demonstrate that any object that scatters light will naturally exhibit specific, inherent patterns of energy absorption. These patterns are unique to each object and do not change even if the object is rotated. Furthermore, we found that these eigenchannels can be used as a basis for decoding complex optical messages and for empowering solar cells to identify and ignore unwanted forms of light.

We've conducted an experiment to find the optimal subset of weights for a conventional neural network with hidden layers, and compared the results to one trained using convolutional and fully connected layers. Interestingly, removing some conv and fc layers and fine-tuning the remaining network often yields better performance than training it from scratch. This suggests that a well-chosen subset of a conventional neural network, with fewer hidden layers, can outperform the more complex, layer-specific model.

In the field of computational neuroscience, the process of learning can be represented as a path that navigates through a landscape of memories, progressing from less to more proficient skills. The quality of a student's skills is evaluated by two measures: the actually acquired skills (already known) and the anticipated skills (in the process of being learned). Inspired by this concept, this research proposes a statistical model to quantify the anticipated value of a portfolio of investments. The model suggests that the portfolio's value can be estimated by the average return expected from each investment, similar to how a learner's proficiency is evaluated by its training progress. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses existing methods in predicting the portfolio's future performance, while also revealing a common pitfall in these traditional approaches. Furthermore, this research develops an efficient algorithm for determining the optimal portfolio sizes, which significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in both efficiency and investment strategy. The model and algorithm are theoretically grounded in a large ensemble of random experiments, providing a non-conservative bound on the possibility of achieving a specified level of return with current investment options.

This work builds on our previous research (arXiv:2101.02791), where we developed a new method for calculating the critical dimension of a general $O(N)$ symmetric theory with a scalar field of a specific type at specific points. Using the same techniques, we successfully calculated the same critical dimension for all $O(N)$ values in the range from 2 to infinity at the $E_6$ fixed point in a specific type of $O(N)$ field configuration, an achievement that was previously not reported in any academic publication. Additionally, we identified the general form of a critical dimension in an $O(N)$ theory for any $O(N)$ value and field configuration type across various orders of loop counts.

This research explores the effect of different mechanisms of electron-phonon interaction on valley dynamics within a two-dimensional lattice model comprising of two atoms per unit cell, where symmetry-allowed and symmetry-forbidden optical phonons between valleys are accounted for. Investigating optical valley Hall effects and inter-valley transition rates in a 2D material, where intravalley scattering is negligible, has revealed that a critical mechanism facilitating inter-valley transitions among these symmetrically interacting valleys is the inversion of electron-phonon coupling in a symmetric environment. Additionally, this study delves into the balance of inter-valley and intra-valley scattering rates in 2D materials under varying temperatures.

We successfully applied our 1st place method, DOMMA, to the NeurIPS 2022 VisDA Challenge to adapt models across different domains. Although the competition rule stated that feature extractors couldn't be fine-tuned, our approach involved two networks trained in parallel: a fixed feature extractor and a domain-adaptation classifier. By leveraging domain features from the input data and combining them with the representation from the fixed feature extractor, our approach effectively adapted models to new domains. Additionally, our method reduced the training time of the domain-adaptation classifier by 85% through the use of synthetic data generated via style transfer.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. The algorithm's success in its standard form is conditional on the data being flat in high dimensions. In cases where data is curved or circular, as with data involving directional information, applying t-SNE yields suboptimal results. Incorporating directionality into the process through the use of direction-based distributions like the von Mises-Fisher (VMF) distribution can maintain the algorithm's key advantage – preserving local similarities – while enabling the analysis of spherical data. Building on this understanding, we introduce VMF-SNE, creating a t-SNE-like representation for spherical data and comparing its performance to alternative approaches.

We utilize the innovative tool of Diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DMC) introduced by Christian (Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 110401, 2016), to study the characteristics of the Fermi polaron in two-dimensional (2D) space. The approach leverages an iterative numerical method based on Euler rotation to handle the Schwinger operator formalism and efficiently generates an approximate Eulerian propagator. Our results confirm that the polaron zero-binding energy occurs at the critical coupling $\lambda_c$ where the effective mass approaches infinity. Additionally, we calculate the critical coupling for which the effective one-particle Schrödinger equation has at least one bound state as $\lambda_c^{2D} \approx 0.0702$. Compared to the available 2D analytical solution, our findings exhibit $\lambda_c^{2D} \approx 0.070$$. Furthermore, we explore the momentum distribution $n_\mathbf{k}$ of the polaron and establish that its asymptotic large-momentum behavior is proportional to $\mathbf{k}^2/\lambda$, which is consistent with predictions from both the large-deformation variational theory and the small- $\lambda$ perturbation analysis.

We investigate the quantum simulation of Fermi-particle systems using the hybrid digital-analog approach and find that this method effectively deals with system complexities, despite the limited number of digital qubits available. The efficient use of analog qubits and quantum measurements enables the simulation of Fermi-particle behavior through the analysis of digital-analog circuits' characteristic parameters. This method can serve as a useful criterion for evaluating the feasibility of simulating Fermi-particle systems on quantum computers.

Graph characteristics refer to polynomial-based entities such as invariants, equations, and partitions, which provide a concise way to describe a given graph. In this context, the focus lies on global graph characteristics - polynomials that evaluate to the same value for isomorphic graphs. We delve into the fundamental properties of such characteristics, which can be seen as a type of 'universal coding' for graphs. Given that infinite series of polynomials are a natural expression of graph characteristics, we explore the conditions under which the infinite series of a graph characteristic converges. Additionally, the article also discusses the inverse problem of proving a given infinite series is a graph characteristic. Our discussion is grounded in contemporary research, which includes results from the works of Iwanow, the Brown-Eisner-Zentner conjecture, and corrections to Galvin's conjecture regarding the connection between symmetric polynomials and the homomorphism polynomial.

The moduli space of one-forms on a genus g curve has a well-documented structure as a mixture of an affine building's chambers and a separate complex that resembles a grassmannian. An extended region, known as the Veech curve, has a corresponding set of isogenies that transitions through a particular sequence of singularities, mapping from an upper level to a lower level in this moduli space. Our research focuses on a normal genus 2 curve and identifies an arrangement of lines that fully enclose the Veech curve at the lowest level of this moduli space, revealing themselves to be components of a singular rational variety and a specific type of geometric object known as an algebraic link. Additionally, our definitions and proofs of specific geometric objects, including the Veech curve, singularities, and particular arrangements of lines, are grounded in the principles of algebraic geometry.

This study investigates how remote work affects the success of software projects using Scrum framework by examining both the Project Management Maturity and Scrum Implementation Questionnaire metrics. Employing a quantitative approach, data from 37 projects involving 221 developers was analyzed to compare co-located and distributed teams. Additionally, interviews with 32 developers provided qualitative insights. Our findings indicate that distributed teams struggle with collaboration and communication, but ultimately achieve equal results with co-located teams in terms of project outcomes.

The study introduces a concept called Gau-Wu values. For a selected arrowhead matrix, it is demonstrated that these values can be calculated through the determinant of a specific type of matrix constructed from its eigenvalues, akin to the method for a symmetric matrix previously explored. Furthermore, a new approach is presented to determine the Gau-Wu values of a 4x4 matrix, utilizing its maximal and minimal eigenvalues as well as diagonal elements, demonstrating that these values can also be expressed as the determinant of a related matrix to the unitary matrix composed of eigenvalues. Ultimately, some distinct properties related to the Gau-Wu values of a class of special matrices, including symmetric, skew-symmetric, skew-symmetric block, and arrowhead matrices, are established and discussed.

Research measured the elliptic flow of particles created when lead nuclei collide at a specific energy level in a laboratory setup. Data from this study were combined with data from another experiment, yielding results for numerous particles. An analysis found that the elliptic flow of some particles varies based on the direction of the event, a phenomenon known as a systematic movement. This study further examined the connection between particles produced in certain areas and the direction of the event. It found that particles produced closer to the event's midpoint have less elliptic flow. An theoretical model, which assumes that particles interact under specific physical conditions, was able to interpret these results.

In 2018, Connes and Lescop introduced the concept of steadfast homology as a specialization of extended homology relevant to chromatic spectral sequences. The purpose of this work is to apply the concept of steadfast homology to the study of chromatic alpha structures, a concept originating from early work by Friedan and Windey, with later developments by Lescop, Connes, and Lescop. By doing this, we establish steadfast homology as a versatile tool for these studies. Additionally, a well-known theorem by Quillen enables us to link the steadfast homology of a space with the homotopy groups of a space, showing that the former can be used to determine the latter. As an application of this relationship, we can use steadfast homology to define an equivalent measure of the homotopy type of a chromatic alpha structure. The work also defines a generalized stable homotopy group and shows its equivalence to the generating series of steadfast homology of a space. With this framework, we can use computational methods to determine the generating series of steadfast homology for some specific spaces.

This research investigates the extreme growth potential of communications in multi-user interference networks with distributed power control.  Earlier work showed that an optimal power schedule in a K-user system can lead to a significant improvement in capacity growth, with better results than a binary power schedule for large K.  Prior work estimated this improvement in terms of binary power schedule's growth rate, plus an additional logarithmic order term.  Contrary to the expectation that the best possible growth rate would decrease as K increases, this study shows the opposite: the difference in growth rates, multiplied by the logarithm of the number of users, is proportional to the square root of K.

Maintaining the trust in experts' conclusions is crucial, especially when they evaluate the credibility of medical tests or financial reports. A decision-making system for auditing has been developed, utilizing an adaptive learning approach to classify risky situations or normal circumstances. This algorithm adjusts its concept hierarchy model by evolving the context over time, allowing for incremental learning. Additionally, a method to assess the expertise's overall accuracy has been proposed, incorporating formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory's framework.

The Strauss model, a type of point process, is often used to model areas with a relatively sparse and non-uniform distribution of points. Generating random samples from this model can be a complex and computationally time-consuming task, which is the focus of this study. By dividing the study area into smaller sections, we can use existing information from each zone to create new, usable areas and repeat the process to generate a set of points that accurately represent the non-uniform distribution of the study area. Our method, known as stitching, combines these new areas to create a set of points that can be used to model the study area's point pattern. Our methodology involves breaking down the study area into smaller sections, generating random samples within each area to create new, usable point patterns, and repeating the process to generate a set of points that accurately represent the study area's point pattern. Our method serves as a reference for simulating the Strauss model. Additionally, we tested our method in different contexts, including from thinning a Poisson process and two practical data sets, the African fruit bat and the coral fish data. Our results show that our method successfully generates realistic and computively efficient samples for both the Strauss model and the point pattern itself. Our method is available through a R-coverage, R-ESM, and Python packages through emspat, emspatR, and emspatpy to facilitate replication and extension.

In the context of string theory, the generalized uncertainty principle reveals a modification in position measurements that leads to an asymptotic deviation from the Planck principle. This modified principle is formulated as $\Delta x \geq \frac{\hbar}{\Delta p}+A_{G}\Lambda_{G}$, where the term $A_{G}\Lambda_{G}$ represents a correction related to a thermodynamic entropy function and fundamental length $L_{G}$, also known as the Planck length. The study aims to investigate the potential effects of this modified uncertainty principle on space and time alterations, utilizing the extended relativistic kinematics model as the primary framework. The Lorentz transformation is re-evaluated to determine if the modified uncertainty principle leads to a shift from special to general relativity, and to clarify the relationship between the fundamental length $L_{G}$ and coordinate $\xi$.

We're investigating a new problem, Multitasking Time Table Adjustment (MTTA). A certain type of timetable problems have adjustable elements which contribute to their solving complexity. Many instances of these problems arise in real-life with limited time frames and need to be solved efficiently. Our MTTA framework simulates such situations by combining n distinct timetable problems. To tackle MTTA, we developed a generic solver utilizing Constraint Programming with spontaneous reflection, enabling the encoder to translate each problem into the solver's language. Our results demonstrate that using a shared solver is more efficient than individual solvers for each single problem instance. Additionally, using a distributed framework leads to better performance than using a framework on a single machine.

A simplified model for the hopping motion of a one-legged robot is simulated on a deformable surface by treating it as a mass-supported pendulum with feedforward motion control. To maintain control over its motion, the robot utilizes a specific trajectory planning strategy based on the desired trajectory, which remains unchanged throughout the hopping process. Since this simple planning strategy does not involve feedback from the system, it significantly reduces computational complexity in simulation. By utilizing this planning strategy, we were able to accurately match the dynamics of a one-legged robot as simulated on a one-dimensional spring-like medium and two-dimensional soft ground generated using the Discrete Element Method (DEM). Furthermore, we explored other parameters that affect the robot's motion by simulating it using different masses, lengths, and ground stiffnesses. Ultimately, we were able to identify specific combinations of these parameters that allow the system to hop in a quasi-periodic motion, which has been observed in robots that actually walk on soft ground.

To minimize disruptions and keep dependencies intact, routine maintenance tasks like network node relocations and device repairs must be executed carefully. Additionally, implementing trustworthiness in networks of devices is essential for maintaining reliability, and this is particularly true for the process of updating device firmware, which is a critical aspect of device management. The installation of new firmware on devices is a delicate operation that requires careful planning to avoid causing chaos in the network, and this is especially true for the process of updating device firmware, which is a precise calculation. A study that analyzed reliable mesh network protocols by collecting data from over 1000 nodes in real-time was conducted, and this research provides essential evidence to support the feasibility of reliable firmware updates in large networks of devices.

We employ a recursive Green function approach to compute the full Fock space propagator and analyze its Aslamov-Solov'ev fractal dimension across the many-body localization phase diagram. Our results indicate that this dimension serves as a indicator of the eigenstate's entanglement density by measuring the number of tunnelling paths between different entanglement segments, with the phase transition to many-body localization being characterized by power-law behavior in the critical phase. Moreover, we observe that fractional dimensions exhibit multifractal properties with a root cause originating from the lattice rather than being an intrinsic aspect of the eigenstates.

This paper investigates a novel problem called multi-object interactive search, where an agent needs to locate several undetected markers in an unknown environment by asking informative queries. The key constraints in this scenario include the limited availability of both the agent and the environment for question-asking, and the presence of noisy responses from the environment. To address this issue, a novel query-asking strategy is proposed, which prioritizes noisy information evaluation to maximize chances of finding all the hidden markers at the optimal cost. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of search strategies is conducted, showing that using noisy data can significantly reduce the query count compared to non-interactive searching, and even compare favorably to optimal interactive search methods in certain cases, while also deriving a fundamental upper limit on the query count for multi-target interactive search.

Researchers have discovered a novel approach to evaluate the robustness of quantum machine learning models by manipulating the input data, but its application is limited to local attacks. In contrast, our work presents a more comprehensive framework that enables both local and global assault strategies. By generating adversarial examples using the Linear Programming method, we show that quantum classifiers are more susceptible to attack when faced with hostile data both within and beyond their native space. Furthermore, we display the adversary-generated samples graphically and compare their similarity to original data in the intra-space context. In addition, we found that quantum models perform equally poorly when confronted with either intra- or inter-space disturbances, but our analysis using Qmetrics reveals that they behave unpredictably when exposed to various levels of noise. Finally, we hope the source code provided will inspire future research into quantum classification noise resilience.

We're studying Steklov eigenvalues associated with almost spherical domains.  Specifically, we focus on two-key aspects:  First, how do these eigenvalues relate to isometric transformations?  In other words, if we apply a change of coordinates to a domain, how do the Steklov eigenvalues change?  We derive the precise formulas for these transformations, known as cohomology versions of Kottler's formulas.  Our work extends earlier research on flat surfaces and signals that these formulas apply broadly across surfaces of negative curvature as well.  In the second key aspect, we prove that Steklov eigenvalues can identify almost spherical regions geodesically.  Our result is a logical extension of the classification theorem for regions with positive curvature by Systermans.  In a broader context, we explore the connections between almost spherical regions, regions with positive curvature, and regions with negative curvature in a shared geometric framework.

We've established a precise framework for verifying compliance with trace segments by leveraging the notions of infix and postfix alignments. This framework's strength lies in its ability to be applied to both deterministic and non-deterministic systems. The concept of postfix alignment in finite trees, including traces, is central to our verification method, allowing it to accurately measure the distance between two states even in non-deterministic scenarios. Through the incorporation of a well-established problem known as Postfix-2-Hypoynteras, our framework establishes a connection between compliance verification and reachability problems in trace segments, offering insights into the complexity of compliance verification. This complexity analysis reveals that compliance verification has a computable upper bound equal to the size of the trace segment and trace alignments, specifically O(traces^3), making it computationally feasible. Moreover, we've demonstrated that determining the existence of an infix alignment has a computational complexity of P, establishing a pivotal connection between compliance verification and its foundational component, infix alignment. This relationship holds significant importance in practical compliance verification cases, which involves verifying the compliance of two traces with a predetermined sub-trace.

Accurate prediction of signal strength is essential for ensuring quality of service in modern cellular networks.  This is a complex task due to the diverse range of frequencies and environmental conditions involved.  In this research, a high-performance deep neural network model is developed for predicting signal strength in diverse cellular network settings.  A large dataset consisting of 9,000 randomly generated signal scenarios is employed for training the model.  By leveraging the advantages of deep neural networks, this model can predict signal strength quickly and accurately in various low-altitude, wide-band propagation environments.  Validation and verification of the model involve comparing its predictions to established measurement standards and the results of computer simulations.  In terms of error statistics, the model's performance is comparable to that achieved using established propagation models.

This research presents a precise semantics for temporal planning, serving as a foundation for future developments, and outlines the necessary requirements for a planning system to adhere to this semantics. Additionally, it formally verifies the correctness of a validation procedure for temporal planning, marking the first instance of formal validation in the field. The proposed semantics provides a common language for comparing model checkers and offers opportunities for future validation. The validation procedure is based on the model checkers' inability to discover planning violations, and proof of its correctness relies on the fundamental properties of planning algorithms. Since many temporal planning systems have not been formally validated, we conducted an experiment to assess their compliance with the established semantics. The evaluation, performed with seven leading planning systems, revealed four components where the semantics semantics led to differences in output compared to the original systems: time point representation, duration comparison, propositional simplification, and metric temporal logic. The study found one system fully compliant with the specified semantics and two others requiring modifications to fully align, while four systems required modifications to accurately implement the semantics for all features. The discovered issues with the systems' behavior have been passed on to the system developers for review.

Power grid models are employed to decide whether to upgrade or maintain the existing network, 
or invest in new energy infrastructure. Various methods have been proposed for modeling network 
expansion, each with its own strengths and limitations. To facilitate comparisons, a universal framework 
is introduced to evaluate the responsiveness of these models to different energy mixes and investment 
 Strategies. This framework considers the optimal network configuration under distinct assumptions 
about energy mix, transmission lines, and generating capacity. Furthermore, an iterative refinement 
mechanism is presented to enhance model accuracy. The framework's practicality is demonstrated through 
applications to a 2000-bus European power grid model and a 3378-bus American power grid model.

The model in question is relevant to plasma and stellar physics, featuring a plasma particle distribution function denoted by $f_t(x,\xi)$, where $x$ represents position, $\xi$ momentum, and $t$ time. Given that the plasma contains a single charge, the Vlasov-Poisson system incorporates the Vlasov equation for $f_t(x,\xi)$ and the Poisson equation for the electric potential $\phi_t(x)$. Concept positioning tasks require defining and categorizing open-text entries based on specific usage contexts. Search term recognition, a key part of this process, involves identifying search queries as concept positioning inputs. In this study, we developed a novel approach - Strict, which employs retrieval-based models to learn a search term recognition model for concept positioning. Our approach is unique because it doesn't necessitate comprehensive search queries for training. Instead, it can utilize partially exposed queries, allowing it to outperform alternative models that were trained with full queries.

Researchers previously discovered that applying ultrasonic vibrations to colloidal gels weakens their structure, enabling the gels to flow once they exceed a specific threshold stress. Our investigation aimed to further explore this phenomenon by examining how gel structure, particle size, and the presence of architectural order within the gel affect ultrasonic exposure. Our findings reveal that in gels with a high density of connected particles, ultrasonic vibrations lead to a significant increase in deformity and internal friction, while gels with isolated clusters show primarily mechanical adaptation rather than significant changes in structure. Moreover, our research indicates that ultrasonic vibrations can repair damage to the gel structure caused by external forces, potentially extending the gel's lifespan. In addition, we found that altering particle characteristics or adding architectural order within the gel completely reverses its responsiveness to ultrasonic vibrations. These findings reveal that manipulating local particle behavior under stress transforms the gel's overall rheological and flow characteristics, which are normally inactive, thereby exposing latent properties. These findings also demonstrate that a material with seemingly inactive properties can be manipulated through the introduction of a secondary energy source, a concept that could be applied to other materials.

To effectively classify STEM documents, multiple categories must be defined, 
which can be challenging due to the documents' casual presentation. Typically, 
classifications focus on either the overall content or the structure of the documents 
as opposed to combining both for accurate categorization. This study aims to improve 
document categorization by combining expertise from both content and structure 
specialists through the utilization of mathematical entities and their categorization. 
A new approach has been developed by combining a probabilistic method, specifically 
the Bayesian classifier, for categorization with the integration of both mathematical 
entities and text-based representations of documents, as well as incorporating 
probability based weighting for categorization. Results demonstrate the efficacy of 
this method in automatically categorizing individual documents across multiple categories 
and also show that the combination of diverse document representations leads to an 
enhancement in accuracy.

Deep local descriptors, which create low-level image features, heavily rely on a precise matching process to calculate their distance. Traditionally, the distance between these descriptors was approximated by randomly matching each descriptor in one image with its closest match in the other image, which is both inefficient and inaccurate due to the time complexity of $O(N^2)$, where N represents the total number of descriptors in both images. More recent approaches aim to improve this by directly searching for the five closest matches for each descriptor, but this is still limited by the time complexity of $O(N^3)$. To overcome these limitations, a new approach called Stable Pairing has been developed to ensure a more precise matching process by efficiently matching each descriptor in one image with its top five closest matches in the other image, achieving a time complexity of just $O(N)$ despite working with large datasets. Furthermore, the top five matches can be filtered using a novel approach called Rank Post-Correlation, which calculates each descriptor's post-correlation rank based on the correlation of the descriptor's magnitude and its corresponding top five ranks, effectively reducing false positives and accelerating detection speeds in both still images and real-time video feeds. Extensive testing across 13 diverse datasets shows that the presented framework and novel approaches significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art systems by as much as 65% recalled.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models have significant drawbacks, as they often disagree on which system is better and what constitutes high-quality summaries. To resolve this issue, this paper introduces SummScore, a novel assessment metric that effectively measures the performance of summarization models. Unlike existing methods, SummScore utilizes Contextualized Elbow method, a highly accurate representation model, to provide detailed analysis and identify its weaknesses. Additionally, SummScore incorporates a diversity of reconstruction methods, including non-coverage and coverage, and incorporates a score balancing method to ensure its reliability. Experimental results on the ASSET dataset demonstrate that SummScore outperforms existing evaluation metrics, and its performance is consistent with human assessments. Furthermore, SummScore is proven to provide comprehensive explanations for its assessments, as it can identify and correct flaws in popular summarization models.

A common practice in signal processing involves using a noisy observation that follows a specific formula derived from the signal to be recovered, which typically involves taking derivatives of the signal. The standard approach to achieve optimal results is to gather enough observations to form a positive-definite matrix, which can then be inverted to estimate the signal directly. In this study, when the number of observations is just one, the matrix becomes singular and cannot be inverted easily. The researchers achieved reliable results by adding a specific 'penalty' to the observation when estimating the signal, which is a common mathematical technique known as Tikhonov regularization. The study, however, found that this method does not use the full potential of the observations when estimating signals. To overcome this limitation, a new method was developed that aims to formulate the signal in terms of the observations in the least-squares sense while keeping the observation's structure intact as much as possible. The researchers tested the approach on a specific problem in geophysics known as inverse molybdenum and found that it performed better than Tikhonov regularization in terms of accuracy and the overall condition number of the matrix, which measures how sensitive the results are to changes in the observations. The study's findings are also linked to a common problem in machine learning known as regularized kernel regression and show that, in some cases, incorporating additional information about how much each data point affects others can improve the outcome. The widespread use of autonomous vehicles has led to a heightened interest in 3D perception technology, which utilizes LiDAR data to create in-depth scenes. Despite the capabilities of current LiDAR technology, it is often supplemented by 2D camera data due to different viewing ranges, which can lead to camera and LiDAR synchronisation issues. This synchronization challenge has hindered the development of unified camera and LiDAR perception systems. To address this problem, research into camera and LiDAR fusion has increased, which involves fusing 2D and 3D spatial data to enhance overall perception capabilities. However, existing fusion approaches are often complex, which may cause them to: only work with specific types of sensors; struggle to scale; or fall short in terms of performance accuracy. This research seeks to rectify this by developing a basic and efficient LiDAR-camera fusion framework that is easy to implement and efficient, which also enhances feature extraction and 3D geometry perception capabilities using xCorres for correspondence matching and a unified encoder-decoder structure for 3D geometry reconstruction. The framework was validated using two popular automotive datasets: NDSU_VTS and KITTI_VS, which showed that the results were competitive or superior to other current state-of-the-art approaches.

In thermal media with slight disturbances, the local temperature variation's average time to return to equilibrium is significantly longer than the inverse of the system's Reynolds number, yet this average is proportional to the Reynolds number for high Reynolds flows. A study on the local dynamics in this range identified near-equilibrium, locally homogeneous temperature fluctuations as the primary characteristic, which contradicts classical theories of thermal convection and hydrodynamics. Instead, the work reveals that these fluctuations are similar to the local dynamics in low-Reynolds turbulent flows and identifies two key features: the coexistence of local homogeneous and heterogeneous behaviors and the maintenance of local homogeneity through constant fluxes and gradient coupling. A dynamic model has also been developed, which captures the essential dynamics of the system at certain wavenumbers and predicts the emergence of homogeneous temperature fluctuations, thus providing a framework for understanding high-Reynolds-number turbulent convection and the temperature variation timescale in thermal disturbances at low Reynolds numbers.

Recently, we had the opportunity to examine noncrystalline materials at high laser intensity, which led us to observe self-focusing and nonlinearity-induced diffraction patterns. However, the underlying thermal effects were not taken into consideration in our explanation. This paper builds upon our previous work, where we incorporate the laser absorption loss into the model to better comprehend diffraction patterns. We demonstrate that deflection patterns are a result of a combination of self-focusing, diffractive, thermosensitive, and absorptive effects. Additionally, the model allows for precise calculation of the laser intensity, temperature distribution, and energy absorption within the material.

Interaction design effectively involves crafting well-structured product requirements specifications that consider multiple perspectives, including future users and contexts. Unfortunately, the product development process often overlooks these diverse perspectives, mainly due to a lack of relevant expertise and resources. This study centers on designing a semi-automated approach to extract potential requirements from interactive product usage dialogs, specifically focusing on the 'what' and 'why' aspects. This research aims to address existing practical challenges in requirement extraction by leveraging linguistic analysis and natural language processing. We address two primary limitations by developing solutions for interpretation consistency and interpretation diversity: (1) selecting a set of interpretations with high consistency, (2) expanding the scope of interpretations to enhance diversity. We evaluated our approach on usage dialogs from the Android Open Source Project, comparing it with existing semi-automated methods. The results indicate that our approach yields more comprehensive and diverse interpretations with significantly higher consistency.

We introduce a unified approach for processing intricate streams and cumulative data with dynamic inquiry languages. Our framework, dubbed H-STREAM, is based on a novel logical structure for specifying and coordinating both temporal events and cumulative data. It maintains a streamlined and uniform description of both streaming activities and cumulative data, using a uniform composition technique for merging and coordinating these events and data. The H-STREAM logical structure is employed to build versatile analytics pipelines that can be both executed and persisted, enabling the processing of both streaming data and cumulative information within defined timeframes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of H-STREAM by presenting its application to a real-world problem in disease spread tracking.

Building upon earlier work by Chudnovsky et al., this research presents a novel proof of the Graph Colouring Hypothesis by showing that simple graphs on at least 9 vertices can be coloured with 3 colours when certain structured subgraphs are not present, specifically those created by the union of two chordal graphs sharing a single vertex. This expansion of the hypothesis covers its restriction to graphs with no K4-cliques and provides a more comprehensive interpretation of the "non-resonant" condition previously defined by Gerke, Gogic, and Bulatov.

In neural machine translation, a specific challenge known as the copy mechanism has been developed to enhance performance by allowing models to copy words from external sources when necessary. Building upon this concept, our research addresses a different type of copying requirement found in translating knowledge base content between languages. A significant obstacle in translating knowledge base content stems from the fact that certain concepts within a query are derived from information stored in previous queries or overall knowledge base data. In order to address this, we developed a novel mechanism called the duplicate mechanism which enables translation models to either copy entire knowledge base components as verbatim or reproduce them in a modified form by drawing on broader knowledge base data. In contrast to the copy mechanism, our mechanism differs in that it refers to information management within a single knowledge base as opposed to searching for novel meanings. In order to test this innovation, we created two distinct translation tasks: one involving translating knowledge base content between languages and another involving translating concepts within a knowledge base from one language to descriptive phrases in another language. Experimental findings using this new approach demonstrate that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in translating knowledge base content. All code and tools associated with this research have been made freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/lequille/KBNMTrans.

When evaluating scholars based on citation counts, researchers are overlooked who excelled early in their careers and may no longer be active due to retirement. To provide a more comprehensive evaluation, a more accurate metric is proposed - one that assesses the reputation and impact of the venues where top scholars published their significant research findings. This approach not only adjusts the weighting given to newer contributions but also offers an opportunity to analyze the predictive power of prestigious academic journals and conferences. Using regression models, the collective predictive potential of individual venues can be measured and contrasted with citation-based metrics, highlighting their limitations. The results demonstrate that collectively, the collective predictive power of approximately 5% of the extensive network of academic venues can account for about 60% of variance in total citations received. Moreover, cross-validation procedures show that cross-applying these models results in roughly 50% loss in explanatory power. Consequently, relying solely on citation-based metrics is shown to result in the misclassification of around 33% of scholars in scenarios where venues are given due consideration.

To accomplish this, we use a combination of reachability analysis and learning, which enables us to verify these controllers not just under normal conditions but also in response to unforeseen scenarios and system failures. Our novel approach to validation is based on learning an NN that mimics the behavior of the safety-critical controller, which was initially designed using traditional methods. This validation NN can then accurately apply the original safety-critical instructions, including compliance with specified safety rules, by learning them from the original controller. Our proposed learning algorithm in this research extends the concepts of adversarial training and backward simulation, which enables us to learn the inverse mapping of the safety-critical controller. Our approach to validation has been successfully tested on two complex case studies: (a) a vehicle with autonomous steering, which was applied to autonomous driving, and (b) control of a drone with failure-induced uncertainties, which was inspired by military requirements.

Scientific and engineering applications require efficient clustering algorithms that can efficiently process large datasets in near-linear time, regardless of the data size. Although existing methods provide good clustering for specific tasks, they fall short for other applications. To address this, a new approach called Funnel Clustering is proposed, which is the first fully functional, available implementation of a time-efficient (near-linear time complexity) clustering algorithm for large datasets with overlapping groups. With a universal design, Funnel works on any type of numerical data without pre-requisites, and is capable of handling various transformation types without the need for manual adjustment. It is a single-function (monadic) algorithm with a straightforward 'add' interface for inserting points and generates multiple robust, overlapping groupings at different levels, which are saved in time. This is unique from other tree-based clustering methods. Funnel has a single parameter that balances computation time and space with the level of grouping. It is simple to use, with a concise high-level implementation, and is capable of handling millions of data points on a standard laptop, making it suitable for big data processing. To illustrate its efficiency and performance, Funnel Clustering is tested on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its performance in a tabular format. This study showcases Funnel Clustering's simplicity, near-linear time complexity, efficient implementation, and practical performance on both synthetic and real-world data, making it a reliable tool for a wide range of applications.

Many applications in computer vision rely heavily on tensor recovery for reliable data interpretation. The process of recovering undercomplete and low-rank tensor data from local measurements is a critical challenge in the field. Past solutions have mostly been based on non-streaming, dense sampling patterns that are not well-suited for efficient implementation on resource-constrained edge devices due to their high memory usage and slow processing speeds. To overcome these limitations, a new streaming tensor recovery algorithm has been developed that is capable of independently reading in small chunks of data from memory, expanding each chunk into a large tensor, and restoring it accurately. The new algorithm, called Patch Monitoring-based Streaming Tensor Recovery (PASTR), utilizes both local and global data patterns by maintaining a summary of each tensor's factors, and both forward and backward references to its previous and next chunks in a data buffer. By continuously updating this summary using a streaming completion technique, and gradually restoring each chunk based on various criteria, PASTR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in restoring visual data, as demonstrated by its results on synthetic, compressed, and partially missing image datasets.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the Nichols algebra for each traditional Weyl group is too large to be equal to the Drinfeld center of the group's underlying algebra, a claim previously established in a separate study by Dong, Gu and Yan. In particular, the finding proves the conjecture posed in another paper by Dong, Gu and Yan. The finding essentially shows that for most traditional Weyl groups, the Nichols algebra serves as an appropriate generalization of the quantized group algebras associated with these groups, a notion that was previously explored in a separate study by Calvo, Menzel and Zelmanov. The final instance concerns the cases where the groups' orders are 10, 12, or 24. In these instances, it has been previously established that the Nichols algebra is too large to be equal to the Drinfeld center of the group's underlying algebra, a claim made in a separate study by Dong, Gu and Yan.

In computational models simulating inertial wave turbulence in rotating spherical shells, our research confirms that the local spectral density of the kinetic and total enstrophy is accurately represented by the classic Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum. Our findings validate previous theoretical and experimental findings on the subject, and were achieved by utilizing the Kepler lattice search algorithm, a more efficient approach to solving optimization problems compared to the widely used conjugate gradient method.

The field of graph theory has seen substantial growth recent to recent years, reflecting its broad influence across various scientific disciplines. Research in this field is particularly prominent due to its versatility, covering multiple interconnected topics. There has been an increasing focus on comparative studies within graph theory, analyzing how different methods compare when applied to real-world datasets. This work aims to improve the accuracy and efficiency of these studies by introducing a new set of tools referred to as reference sets. Essentially, reference sets are collections of graphs that can be used to standardize and benchmark individual graphs. This is accomplished by generating the reference set directly from a given graph, effectively turning a single graph into a dataset for analysis. This process has the added benefit of providing a baseline performance that can be used for comparison. To validate the introduced tools, we provide theoretical bounds for the size of reference sets, implement the methods on real-world datasets, and analyze the results. Furthermore, we apply the proposed framework to the problem of finding the maximum weighted independent set in a graph, referred to as MWIS. By using reference sets, we enhance existing methods for solving MWIS, resulting in a notable improvement in performance.

This research investigates how the thermodynamic properties of a electrically modulated graphene monolayer change at absolute zero temperature. Using a theoretical framework based on the Landau-Qedernov theory, we studied how an external constant electric field influences the Landau levels within a electrically modulated graphene monolayer. Our analysis derived the thermodynamic quantities, including energy (E), heat capacity (C), entropy (S), and free energy (F), in relation to the external electric field. Our findings show that these thermodynamic quantities exhibit discontinuities at specific critical field intensities, where the energy transfer between the system and its surroundings significantly increases. These critical field intenses correspond to the allowable transmission of electrons through the system at absolute zero temperature. Our research also discovered that the electrically modulated graphene monolayer behaves as a non-standard or unusual physical system due to its unique thermal properties.

Continuous radio emissions from the binary system of CR Draconis, comprised of a flare star and a cooler companion, have been monitored over a nearly 30-year period, during which intense low-frequency bursts and consistent high-frequency emissions were observed. Calculations suggest that radiating electrons must originate from a volume roughly equal to the size of the binary system, with magnetic fields strengthening as the distance from the hotter star increases. Researchers classified the observed radiation into two distinct categories, only one of which could be consistently measured, indicating a complex radio emission mechanism. By analyzing all available data, scientists detected periodic fluctuations in the binary system's radio output, most likely linked to stellar rotation, as well as a significant enhancement near a specific wavelength, which may be influenced by the interaction between the two stars' magnetic fields. They also discovered a notable and relatively brief period of high radio output intensity in 2012, during which time the binary system completed nearly three full rotations. Although the exact cause of this event remains unknown, it is hypothesized to be potentially linked to star-to-star coronal mass ejections.

Achieving visually accurate representations of individuals, often desired in applications like healthcare and film, presents a challenge due to the strict constraints of accurate 3D pose estimation and rendering. The main difficulties arise from the inherent complex dynamics of human movement and the need for a detailed, yield-optimized 3D representation of the subject. Our proposed solution, Articulated Neural Representation (ANR), utilizes a Subject-Object-Environment framework to break down the complex geometry of the avatar into manageable components, which are then encoded using Neural Implicit Functions with respect to key joint positions and orientations. Our approach enables the creation of a compact and precise 3D representation of subjects, allowing for the generation of lifelike avatars from a single image and real-time rendering of dynamic animations, such as walking cycles. Our ANR method demonstrates superior results on existing datasets, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods in both pose estimation and visual reconstruction metrics, while also yielding notable improvements in rendering performance compared to previous methods. The proposed ANR method specifically yields a 6.7 km$^2$ per frame improvement in rendering efficiency for human avatars on the SCAPE dataset, using approximately 0.02 MB per joint to store the neural implicit shape representation.

Deep learning-based image alterations can be performed efficiently but often result in images with artificial appearances that may not resemble authentic content. Our study investigates how much impact a range of intense image modifications have on their visual similarity to original images and how humans and machine vision models perceive these changes. We found that modifying an image through extreme transformations like desaturation or inversion increases its distance from the original image in the embedding space, in line with human judgments. However, transformations like adding noise or applying filters are not as influential. Unlike machines, humans are more tolerant of such minor distortions while still recognizing the underlying content. This suggests that intense image alterations can effectively manipulate how machines and humans perceive images, which has significant implications for applications like image forgery, clustering, search, and content-based indexing.

Utilizing the Poisson summation formula, we derive a formula for the trace of a reduced Chern-Simons partition function with pole locations specified by a link diagram, and this result is reformulated in terms of the trace of a reduced Hamiltonian operator on a closed string. We then demonstrate that the contribution associated with a specific reversible link diagram configuration can be represented as the expectation value of a product of commuting operators that generate the Askey-Wilson algebra, and this expectation value is also the exponential of the Hamiltonian of the Schröder equation. Consequently, the contribution is positive for all configurations, and this result is generalizable to the scenario where the trace is circled, and the associated calculation reduces to the evaluation of the Gaussian integral of the Chern-Simons theory.

We investigate the Monte Carlo quantum behavior of a two-component, spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic lattice formed by connected triangular units with short inter-unit bonds in two-dimensional lattices with short inter-unit connections. Specifically, we study the quantum behavior of these systems in geometric arrangements comprising two interconnecting units and on lattices resembling a square, Kagome, and oblique lattice structures. Our studies focus on the quantum behavior of these systems when the strength of the inter-unit coupling decreases in comparison to the within-unit coupling, where maximum coupling strength serves as a reference point. Our investigation reveals that for weak inter-unit coupling, the system exhibits a highly entangled spin ground state forming a coherent whole upon approaching the point where all units become isolated from one another. However, for stronger inter-unit coupling, the system exhibits multiple spin degrees of freedom forming fractals in a ground state separating into distinct components. Moreover, our studies show that a significant change in the spin ground state of this system from a fragmented to a fractional one occurs at a relatively low critical ratio of the inter-unit coupling. Our research demonstrates that this two-component, weakly-coupled spin-1/2 system on a two-dimensional Kagome lattice exhibits a ground state characterized by large-scale spin correlations without exhibiting a signature of antiferromagnetic ordering on the boundary of a separate non-fractal magnetic phase with inherent spin degrees of freedom.

Recent breakthroughs in zero-shot learning utilizing pre-trained language models show great potential, but the method to achieve this has not been fully understood. This research delves into the model's capabilities, investigating if pre-trained models can learn to identify objects solely based on natural language descriptions. It's demonstrated that current models are primarily skilled at recognizing objects based on descriptions rather than senses. To improve the model's performance in identifying objects based on senses, a new approach called meta-tuning is developed. This method tunes the model's sense-specific classification abilities by meta-tuning it with a comprehensive range of descriptive data from various sources. Moreover, it selects and refines the most relevant data for each sense-based classification task, resulting in an improved model that effectively learns to identify objects based on natural language descriptions and senses alike, thereby expanding its capabilities in zero-shot learning.

In-depth investigations into the NMSSM model's theoretical framework, particularly its aspects that deviate from the Standard Model in a $Z_3$-invariant context, are conducted, including an examination of how these variations impact the electroweak precision measurements. The researchers utilized global fits to the EWPT data that considered the LHC search results, especially focusing on the dark matter stability and its compatibility with the solar neutrino event. The outcomes reveal that, at the 95\% confidence level, the LHC search results substantially restrict the parameter space, while the solar dark matter event leaves a larger, yet compatible area. Furthermore, the authors discovered that for a significant number of the model's parameters, the Gravitational Wave signals produced by the dark matter are predicted to be stronger than those from the first-order phase transition required to initiate the cosmic reionization, indicating the potential for GWS detection with upcoming GW experiments. The experiments may not only confirm the occurrence of the phase transition but also reveal signs of the NMSSM model's features, such as the presence of the light Higgs boson or additional non-vector-like dark matter particles, which could be discovered at the 5-sigma confidence level.

Photometrically stable sources are crucial for making precise astrophysical measurements and reducing uncertainties associated with time variations in optical and near-infrared observations. Radio and millimeter-wave observations of selected sources are continuously monitored as part of the ALMA/Studiu de Fluxi Longmires (SFL) program, which enables the accurate measurement of radio and millimeter-wave light curves with high precision. However, ongoing research reveals that some sources exhibit unexpected time-variable behavior in these wavelengths, which poses a significant challenge to these measurements. To resolve this issue, a novel algorithm called High-z Sudoku has been developed to identify robust changes in millimeter-wave spectra by differentiating between variable and stable sources, thereby enabling the selection of sources with the most predictable behavior for in-depth study. This algorithm's effectiveness is illustrated through its application to two powerful radio sources, 3C454.3 and 3C279, which demonstrates its potential for identifying robust changes in millimeter-wave spectra, enabling the accurate measurement of millimeter-wave light curves, and ultimately informing astrophysical modeling and data analysis in these sources.

A new computational study employs a complex of platinum and gold to replicate the properties of a specific antiferromagnetic material, such as YBaO and HoBaO, in order to simulate the formation of two distinct phases, including one phase that destroys the structural symmetry, by manipulating the strength of its magnetic interactions in a specific geometric arrangement. Our analysis reveals that when interactions of the same intensity are present, the most stable phase exhibits antiferromagnetic order with a specific pattern of magnetic alignment, but this phase transitions into a structurally asymmetric and dynamically normal phase with increasing magnetic order when different interactions occur, characterized by a specific length scale, a rapid decrease in energy quanta, and the presence of magnetic fluctuations. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the dynamic signatures of these phases can be predicted with precision and accuracy from a specific formula that takes into account these magnetic interactions and their correlation, providing valuable insights to experimental researchers on how to identify and distinguish between these phases in real-time.

Following our earlier discovery of the restriction-derestriction transition in SU(3) Higgs theory, this study further explores the dynamics of the theory through effective field theories, at a fixed point that governs the transition dynamics, and provides insight into the breaking patterns of global symmetries in the process.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits an N\'eel temperature of 565 K, making it a key material for studying antiferromagnetism in light elements. Using the unique properties of nuclear magnetic resonance, in-plane magnetic arrangement was confirmed in Cr$_2$Al. The data match theoretical predictions from a Heisenberg framework better than an exchange-coupling framework. Considering the similar parameters in Cr$_2$X (where X = In, Ga, Sn), Heisenberg-like behavior is likely the common case among these materials. Furthermore, the magnetic moment observed in Cr$_2$Al is significantly reduced when compared to other similar materials, such as Cr$_2$In. This difference in moment is attributed to the less-effective exchange-coupling mechanism in Cr$_2$Al. It was also found that moments do not average to zero at temperatures below the N\'eel temperature, which supports the presence of long-range magnetic order in Cr$_2$Al.

A new kinetic model, the speed-dependent model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator for rarefied monatomic gases. The model's collision frequency is adjusted in relation to velocity, reflecting variations in molecular interactions while maintaining consistency with the Chapman-Enskog expansion's transport coefficients. The collision frequency's parameters can be calculated through a method that emulates the phononic properties of binary collisions and thereby accounts for long-range potentials in addition to short-range potentials. The model's ability to accurately predict transport properties for various gas mixtures was demonstrated in multiple studies (Veerbeek et al., 2012; Venskovic et al., 2013; Venskovic, 2015). In this paper, we examine gas flows with diverse collision models depending on velocity, using a method that corrects second-order fluxes while maintaining the underlying kinetic model. The model's application to predict flow patterns around a cylinder at a mean kinetic height of 10, in both smooth and rough surfaces, as well as in flat plate boundaries at different wall materials, reveals a high degree of accuracy and consistency with Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data. Additionally, we observed that the model's accuracy is influenced by the speed-dependent model parameters and collision models used. In order to broaden the scope of applicable collision models, we introduced a simplifying procedure that 'Boltzmannizes' the various models within a single framework, as a means of further developing

We demonstrate that the performance of the semantic analyzer in Transformers can significantly be improved by adjusting the learning process. The analyzer's initial configuration is based on the Universal Sentence Encoder, which was trained on a large corpus of sentences. However, this pre-trained model may not accurately reflect the specific application domain due to the limitations of corpora such as the English Wikipedia. Therefore, we propose two methods for 'familiarizing' the analyzer with the current domain. The first method involves re-training it using an extensive, domain-specific dataset that is available. Although this approach requires substantial computational resources and time, it is effective in improving performance. The second method is more efficient as it leverages the analyzer's ability to accurately process a limited number of carefully selected training samples. This adaptive learning process ensures that the analyzer fills in the knowledge gaps it has upon initializing it from the Universal Sentence Encoder. The analyzer's modified learning process can be used with any pre-trained semantic analyzer, thereby enhancing its performance in the context of the current domain. This research was supported by funding from the Spanish Government (PID2019-21300), the Generalitat Valenciana (GV), and the European Union (ERDF).

Researchers are currently engaged in developing advanced technology for the Electron-Ion Collider, an esteemed future facility that will be responsible for understanding quantum chromodynamics and revealing the mysteries of quarks and gluons in extreme conditions.  A cutting-edge design for a silicon tracker has been proposed, incorporating advanced technology in silicon sensors and advanced materials, designed to handle the intense radiation generated by the high-energy collisions at the EIC.  This research paper will focus on the development of the tracker concept and will discuss the technical advancements in silicon technology and material science that are the foundation of the tracker's design.

A unique case study involves the 10 million solar mass black hole at the center of the galaxy M82, which is known to exhibit extremely intense and rapid variations in brightness. Conducting a comprehensive observation of this galaxy with a powerful telescope on the ground, we were able to accurately measure how quickly the variability changes in intensity, taking just under 28 minutes to complete. Interestingly, this level of variability is more typical of larger black holes than those of its own class, suggesting the presence of a secondary plasma cloud possibly made up of a type of matter known as Advection-dominated Accretion Flow (ADAF). Although we were not able to pinpoint the direct cause of the variability, it's possible that it's a result of time-varying cloud incursions by this plasma, variations in the surrounding material, or even a sudden release of energy known as a 'outburst.' As a result of our findings, we're left with a question: is M82's low-mass black hole capable of producing such dramatically changing brightness levels, or is there another process at work?

The study presents unique narrow-line spectropolarimetry observed in the HD 58260 star, which, to the authors' knowledge, is the first to directly monitor the radial change of the magnetic field within the star using the FEPOPHYS2 instrument at the Pulkovo observatory, even though a significant portion of the observed time span includes a time when the magnetic field's strength is decreasing at a fast rate. The study provides detailed mean values of the magnetic field for each observation session, moreover, the obtained polarimetric data clearly illustrate the varying magnetic field for each session, with one session standing out due to its noisy data. The researchers specifically investigate how the most fast-decreasing observation compares with other sessions, which, interestingly, has a higher average intensity in the D$_\phi$ channel. The most remarkable finding, in terms of its scientific value, is the varying magnetic field for the HD 58260 star, with a higher magnetic field strength during the most fast-decreasing observation, in contrast to the other sessions. The researchers specifically investigate the varying magnetic field for different intensity Levels in the D$_\phi$ channel, with a higher magnetic field strength during the most fast-decreasing observation, in contrast to the other sessions.
