The evaluation of named entity recognition is significant because it lays the foundation for further processing in natural language analysis. In this work, we have developed an approach to contextual named entity retrieval within articles, where entities are first identified through a large termling system and then refined using a context-specific word significance metric that adapts to complex naming patterns, including compound names. Our proposed method presents a practical solution to this critical language processing component, requiring minimal human involvement and adaptable to diverse entity classes. Our results demonstrate contextually retrieved entities to be at least as relevant as those retrieved statically, and our context-free approach was shown to be comparable to state-of-the-art static entity retrieval methods. Building upon this research, we plan to integrate our method with a document collection that is currently being annotated, aiming to reduce annotation reliance by only acquiring context-specific entities. Additionally, we will investigate acquiring entity links, rather than simply names, to provide an extra layer of practical value to this research.

The emergence of COVID-19 has highlighted the significance of time-sensitive data, necessitating the exploration of new methods to visualize and interact with such information efficiently. Researchers and practitioners have adapted various interactive visualization techniques to address the intricacies of long-lasting COVID-19 data. This research aims to identify particular difficulties in visualizing time-sensitive data and related temporal information, in addition to longitudinal information. It then outlines potential interactions in this context, focusing especially on the spatial visualization of multivariate time-based data, to create engaging experiences for users. This study conducts a study with experts to gather feedback on the identified themes, ultimately leading to the formulation of research questions to advance more targeted visualization studies in this area.

The value of disease prediction using artificial intelligence has long been recognized. Researchers are specifically interested in developing reliable AI solutions that translate into real-world clinical decisions. In this paper, we showcase a novel model, the diverse similarity graph neural network (DSGNN), which effectively leverages electronic health records (EHRs) to facilitate disease diagnosis. The integration of dynamic graph attention mechanisms into DSGNN captures the intricate relationships between EHR features and their sequential influences. Experimental results indicate that DSGNN achieves a competitive performance comparative to state-of-the-art methods on a diverse sepsis dataset from a Chinese hospital. What's more, our model accurately identifies sepsis in complex hospital environments while meeting the stringent criteria for practical clinical applications in resource-constrained settings.

Within electric double layers surrounding charged flexible membranes, the presence of solvents displaying induced dipolar properties has long been overlooked, leading to the creation of local electric fields that interact with the membrane in a temperature-dependent manner. Through a combination of chemical potential and a flexible interface model, which considers both internal and external forces, the influence of electric fields generated by solvents on the membrane's structural properties has been examined. Results indicate the physisorption of ions at the membrane, stemming from the induced electric field, is strengthened by the polarization of the solvent. Consequently, the membrane's elasticity is affected as it accommodates the altered pressure within the inner electric double layer. Furthermore, the presence of solvents leads to the reduction of electrolyte ions within the inner electric double layer and an increase in the counterion density within the outer electric double layer. The solvent's influence also shifts the equilibrium swelling state of the membrane and modulates its structural parameter. The observed findings hold significance for understanding the biological flexibility and thickness of cell membranes.

To enhance software development methods, future research aims to leverage
textual information to gather specifications, requirements, and feedback from
various platforms, such as software discussion forums and crowdsourcing sites.
The goal is to pinpoint key requirements and decisions made at any project stage
without interrupting the development process, thus enabling more efficient
verification and improvement of software systems.

This research investigates enhancing the energy efficiency of wireless networks by introducing a method of joint power optimization that works in conjunction with relay allocation. By applying this approach to a specific network topology, we can minimize the total energy consumption while maintaining a required data transfer rate. Initially, we develop an approximate solution for determining optimal power levels, considering each user's direct connections. However, in order to account for the entire network, we introduce a more sophisticated approach known as successive null space programming (SNP), which allows us to optimize both power levels and relay participation simultaneously. Despite SNP's potential to yield nearly optimal results, its computational complexity can be considerable, making it less suitable for real-world applications. In response to this, we present a two-stage approximation method that yields a more efficient solution. First, we determine the optimal relay participation by solving a simplified version of the SNP problem. Next, we apply the obtained relay configuration to calculate optimal power levels. Simulation results indicate that our proposed method offers a substantial improvement in energy efficiency while maintaining acceptable levels of spectral resources.

Utilizing the theoretical framework initially proposed in [Phys. Rev. B 97, 134529 (2018)], we evaluate the electronic properties of a Mn atom and Mn dimers situated on the Nb(110) surface. By integrating both YSR state and initial principles concepts, we establish a comprehensive understanding of the YSR state splitting and its polarization characteristics. Specifically, we consider an Mn single atom and each type of Mn dimer (antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic) on the Nb(110) surface. Our theoretical model is grounded in the relativistic many-body Green's function, with the YSR state calculated through the second-order crossover virtual transition between the Mn impurity and the Nb surface. Our results from this investigation match the YSR state observations reported in recent experimental studies [NP 10, LL 19].

This research introduces a novel method for reliable algorithm development, centered on reducing bias in data collection for autonomous vehicle Data-to-Distribution Scan Matching (DDSM). Unlike human involvement in data annotation, which is subject to bias, our approach involves training a Deep Neural Network (DNN) filter to automatically annotate data, thus minimizing the incorporation of biases during training. Since autonomous vehicle data collection often results in significant label shifts without notice, our method ensures that an unbiased policy is maintained throughout data collection and mapping. This leads to reliable map construction and efficient data retrieval. Additionally, we propose a neural network-based strategy to address the challenges of learning an unbiased policy directly. Our method facilitates real-time map construction without degrading performance, whereas existing bias mitigation approaches in DDSM lead to a delay in convergence or a decline in mapping accuracy. Furthermore, our empirical analysis demonstrates that an unbiased policy can be acquired, and the need to make preference-free decisions is not inherently contradictory.

Satellite images often contain diverse information such as man-made structures, vegetation, and irrigation systems. Extracting detailed data from these images is crucial in research on land-use, urban planning, and crop monitoring. Due to the inherent complexity of these images, many deep learning models have been employed to identify objects within satellite imagery. Nevertheless, these networks require substantial computational resources and can generate varying results when faced with image subsets, different regions, or diverse data collections. This paper presents an evaluation of the performance of a simplified edge-detection model, utilizing the Fractals theory, in comparison to established deep learning approaches for detecting edges in satellite images. The findings indicate that this model achieves edge detection comparable to or even surpassing some leading deep learning techniques, while utilizing a fraction of the computational resources required by these networks. This research aims to simplify the process of applying deep learning models in edge detection, reducing computational and storage demands.

A new approach is taking into account the movement of electrons in a solid when determining the near-edge X-ray absorption spectra (XANES). The standard method for calculating XANES involves a rate equation that only considers a solid's electronic configuration, but this method has a limitation because it does not account for changes in the solid's electronic state over time. In contrast, the new framework incorporates a more comprehensive rate equation that includes both electronic configuration and other relevant factors. By comparing the new approach to experimental data and other theoretical models, researchers have found that it more accurately accounts for changes in the solid's electronic state, which is important for understanding certain types of XANES spectra.

This paper introduces the development of a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture known as the Blend GAN, whose primary objective is to classify modulation types by generating artificial signals. The researchers investigate the effectiveness of this architecture in creating realistic signals, particularly its performance when faced with potential vulnerabilities arising from adversarial attacks. To demonstrate its resilience, a comprehensive evaluation is conducted, exposing the system to crafted adversarial examples and analyzing the performance of the Blend GAN under various attack conditions.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is typically done after collecting numerous patient images. Most techniques train on the images from a single data source. We investigated segmenting lesions when switching between different clinical datasets. Three datasets from various clinics were used for the study. It was observed that directly applying models from one dataset to another resulted in poor outcomes. Therefore, we developed a method to train models from scratch using all available images from different clinics. This training approach, utilizing a transfer learning technique, is based on ongoing training, where the model is refined as new data, images from different clinics, are added. When comparing this method to training or repeating the model without new data, we found that training on the combined images from all clinics yielded significantly better lesion segmentation outcomes. This method also reduced the need to recollect patient images, decreased overall processing time, and allowed for smaller training datasets. Therefore, a strategy for training segmentation models that adapts to new data from different sources has been introduced, showing promising results in real-world applications. This method has been shared publicly to facilitate research in the field of neurology and multiple sclerosis.

The concept of duality plays a significant role in various areas of mathematics. This paper examines dual comparisons within the context of ordered sets, abstract lattices, topological spaces, and Kripke models for modal and epistemic logics. The methodology presented leverages comparisons between relation-based models to generate their duals, often employing modal or epistemic interpretations. This study explores the interplay between comparisons and duality by demonstrating examples that illustrate both comparisons and dual comparisons. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that comparing duals can provide new insights into well-known lattices,, including the finite distributive lattices and ordered topological spaces. Additionally, this paper delves into the connections between duality pairs, comparative semantics, and algebraic and topological models.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in analyzing complex data, especially in image and voice recognition. Their ability to be quickly reconfigured and apply high-level patterns makes them ideal for investigating complex systems, but their interpretability is limited due to their black box nature, which hampers trust and incorporation of their findings into expertise. Developing a straightforward explanation for their mistakes is particularly challenging. An innovative method for uncovering a simple framework describing a deep neural network's error in forecasting the evolution of a complex system is presented. This method, despite requiring no alteration to the network, provides valuable insights into its ability to predict long-term behavior and the timing of its predictions versus actual system behavior. It does this by identifying the simplest alternative to the network's forecasting logic. Following the method's application to a deep neural network initially trained on the Lorenz system, it was tested using the chaotic double well problem and successfully modified to fix a previously reported mistake in a complex system model. This framework facilitates collaboration between a deep neural network and other models, allowing for integration of its forecasting information and correction of its errors.

Recent research using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) revealed evidence of in situ core formation within the Dragon Infrared Dark Nebula (IRDN), which corresponds to the Taurus Molecular Cloud (TMC). By employing a temperature-sensitive carbonaceous molecule as a tracer, it was possible to identify individual kernel structures, which are expected to evolve into future massive star-forming cores over the course of 2 million years. This process will likely result in the formation of massive stars with the potential to become O-type hypergiants. What differentiates this finding from previous research is the large number of developing cores within the IRDN, which suggests that cloud growth through accretion is a primary method of star formation regulation in this location. Additionally, it was observed that O-type stars within the TMC have a limited impact on the temperature of the surrounding environment, which indicates that star formation in this cluster is not regulated by external external pressure from other stars.

Popular cosmological simulations, such as Illustris, use sub-grid physics modules to model unresolvable physical processes. These units are typically assumed to operate randomly, but some systems, like dark matter, require a more organized approach. Dark matter serves as a counterexample to random processes, instead accumulating within primordial black holes and other stars. We've modified the PopSyCLE simulator to account for the formation of black holes within stars and the impact of this process on galactic evolution. We've conducted two series of simulations, one with primordial black holes acting as dark energy sources and another with them affecting galactic gas dynamics. We've found that ignoring the consumption of gas by primordial black holes leads to accurate underestimation of black hole mass, but not their influence on galactic evolution, which can be rectified by incorporating the radius at which gas becomes absorbed.

In the course of dynamic studies with numerical simulations, certain mixtures of particles that only slightly overlap with each other are found to gradually reorganize into clusters of rigid wedges, consisting of 3 to 4 particles each, that are oriented perpendicular to specific directions within the system. The internal splaying of these clusters is accompanied by a collective, rhythmic motion of the entire structure. The overall pattern of the wedges shows direction-dependent density fluctuations - specifically, fluctuations are more pronounced along the directions perpendicular to the clusters and less so along the parallel directions. The density waves within the system are Poyting's late-stage phenomenon. The fact that the clusters are rigid and consist of a few particles each enables the easy identification of their orientation. The edges of the clusters touch a network consisting of perpendicular lines that represent the potential walls formed by the density fluctuations within the system. The frequency of the global motion is directly proportional to the size of the wedges and corresponds to the level of the systematic error in the statistical calculations. The size of the wedges can be used to create a universal timer that is based on the particular mixture being studied. The splaying of the clusters is likely a sign of a more extensive system with similar properties.

Large language model fine-tuning has become the go-to method for developing language artifacts, with a growing number of models being trained on ever-expanding datasets. As models become more sophisticated, the potential outcomes of fine-tuning increase, but this raises concerns about the practicality of fine-tuning in terms of computational expense, memory usage and the risk of data leakage. Our unique fine-tuning approach, called Unique Token Adaptation, mitigates these concerns by only adjusting model parameters related to specific tasks and utilizing unique tokens to differentiate between tasks and eliminate the risk of data leakage. In our experiments, UTA outperformed expected results in zero-shot scenarios and significantly improved adaptation results in few-shot and full-finetuning scenarios, demonstrating its superior performance. Our analysis of UTA further revealed the important role that edited tokens play in the model's performance, highlighting the potential for further research into token editing techniques.

The contextually preferential ranking rule type, introduced in 2020, is a notable approach for multi criterion preference ordering generation. It focuses on addressing set addition problems by incorporating additional information from a decision maker to guide the preference ordering generation process. As a result, only contextually preferential ranking rules can guarantee the absence of inconsistent preferences. This study aims to expand the scope of contextually preferential ranking rules by introducing new theoretical foundations and developing the first relational abstract ranking data type capable of accurately modeling contextually preferential ranking rules. This data type's implementation is grounded in existing research, enabling the encoding of preference information and its corresponding context. In addition, we describe a ranking algorithm that effectively assesses contextually preferential ranking rules, along with an illustration of its applications through a simple example use case.

Our investigation focuses on the connection between thermodynamic properties and dynamic behavior in the primary step of glass formation, specifically through the examination of liquid polystyrene. This is achieved by combining precise measurements of volume and temperature alongside existing data on structural relationships and molecular movements. The key finding reveals a direct proportion between volume variations and entropy changes, and at the same time, a proportional relationship is observed between these volume variations and the square of the amplitude of primary relaxation oscillations. The dynamic properties observed in this study are explained using a bi-modal model of molecular movement, supporting the idea that two distinct types of molecular movement are present simultaneously - a fast, coherent movement within well-organized regions and slower, more random movements throughout the liquid.

Current AI language models operate similarly to human language acquisition but often fall short of human performance. To gain a deeper understanding of how these systems process language, we investigate the development of models that improve on previous versions. Our investigation utilizes a dataset of fake stories generated by AI models and examines how a range of architectures handle contradictory statements. The results indicate that a standard transformer model is not effective in filtering out contradictory information, but modifying the model to prioritize accuracy or to learn rules and exceptions can significantly enhance its performance. Our findings imply that a basic iterative update process can lead to the development of more sophisticated models that can accurately handle language. Since this process is similar to how children learn language, our investigation provides insight into the natural progression of language acquisition.

One of the key challenges in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models is optimizing the production process to reduce computation costs while maintaining or improving model performance. Although research has been focused on predicting the next token based on past information, limited studies have been done on looking forward to predict the next token based on future information. This paper introduces a novel look-forward attention module for NMT to improve sequential decoding by utilizing future context for both encoder and decoder states. The proposed module is designed to absorb information from both past and future contexts, making it more effective than traditional attention mechanisms. Experimental results on the IWSLT15 English-to-Japanese dataset show that our method significantly accelerates NMT models by 40.83% and also enhances the BLEU score by 1.14.

We have developed a method to calculate the Kontsevich weights for graphs representing links and curvatures in two and three dimensions. These graphs arise from the geometric configuration of two Lagrangian manifolds with their intersection displaying the specified graph structure. The weights depend on a central object called form factor, which we defined and determined, showing that it doesn't change with the expansion of graph structures. The formula for weights we derived can be applied to various types of symplectic Poisson structures. Moreover, we have found that graphs in low-dimensional spaces tend to simplify certain differential equations related to turbulence.

We analyze the properties of a large number of states in an interacting compactified Kaluza-Klein system at its thermal equilibrium point. By examining both the thermal entropy of this system and the entropy associated with entanglement in its half-space partition, we demonstrate that these two entropies exhibit large-N approximations in line with one another. Notably, our findings align with the holographic duality's thermal and entanglement entropies in a black hole background. Additionally, we establish that the system's ground state entropy also adheres to these large-N approximation conventions. As a result, we speculate that the system's behavior might share commonalities with a system of semiconductors when it undergoes a volume dilation.

This paper seeks to correct several critical errors made by Li et al. in their framework for pricing Asian options, errors that necessitate revising the Theorems 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14, 17 and 18 presented in the paper.

The Sun's surrounding is made of high-energy particles from various cosmic sources.  Observations from space have detected a part of this radiation, and theories suggest that there might be more coming from large clusters of galaxies.  A new estimate of this radiation, based on the density of dark matter in these clusters, shows that there could be a significant amount already present, and thus a space-based telescope should be able to detect it.  This radiation is expected to be a mixture of charged and neutral particles and its energy spectrum could be the key to determining its source.  The intensity of this radiation is anticipated to be the highest around 1-100 GeV, and detecting this radiation at multiple points in time or varying the energy of the particles should reveal whether it's coming from the Sun's magnetic field or large clusters of galaxies.

A novel hypothesis referred to as the primal features hypothesis is presented, suggesting that peculiar features in the large-scale structure of the universe are rooted in primary cosmic ingredients - presumably dark matter - with energies equivalent to the universe's temperature at recombination. We delve into the phenomenon of cosmological particle production, examining it in the context of the primordial standard model, where creation of massive particles occurs primarily through energy gradients following the universe's recombination. The anticipated spectral patterns for these particles, including critical signs such as sidebands and resonant peaks, can be predicted and may serve as indicators for detecting such primordial features. The proposed hypothesis is compatible with current observations of the cosmic large-scale structure and is potentially verifiable by observing the predicted spectral patterns.

This research delves into the inherent properties of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by uncovering their underlying structure. By dissecting the network, it is demonstrated that CNNs consist of interconnected modules, with each module comprising a convolutional and a squeeze-and-explode operation. Additionally, our investigation reveals that the operations within each convolutional module are actually sequential hidden transformations that facilitate information flow, rather than a fixed convolutional operation. This insight is further utilized to create the Hidden Visual-Semantic Projection (HVSP) framework, which aims to attain a rich, multi-level semantic description from an input image. The framework consists of a visual-semantic projection module that performs this task, and is trained using a innovative combination of supervised and self-supervised methods. The effectiveness of our approach is quantified through evaluations on several benchmark datasets, showcasing its superior performance on hierarchical semantic description when compared to baseline models. Moreover, our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on certain datasets and comparable performance on others with respect to general visual recognition tasks. The code to implement this approach has been made available on our GitHub repository.

Previous theoretical studies have focused on the lateral superconducting interaction between localized electrons in high-temperature cuprates, concluding that this interaction is relatively weak.  However, experimental observations of superconductivity in cuprates with extremely low electron densities ($p$ approximately between $9\times10^{21}$ and $20\times10^{21}$ cm$^{-3}$) suggest the presence of a significant attractive interaction between localized electrons.  In order to resolve this discrepancy between theory and experiment, this research investigates whether localized electrons can facilitate attraction by exchanging plasmons or phonons, which has the potential to produce a substantial attractive interaction between localized electrons at low density.  Utilizing a tight-binding model and second-order perturbation theory, this research evaluates the frequency of cuprate superconducting phonons using a long-wave approximation and calculates the contribution of phonons to the interaction between localized electrons in high-temperature cuprates.  The calculation reveals that phonons can produce a substantial attractive interaction between localized electrons in high-temperature cuprates at low density, thus resolving the discrepancy between theoretical predictions and experimental findings.

The MPHIA dataset has enabled the creation of synthetic health insurance datasets, allowing forcausal structures and efficiency assessments within healthcare systems. This study aims to determine the most effective causal graphical structure among those tested, focusing on individual data. Specifically, the layouts of sparse Gaussian Graphical Models and additive noise models have been analyzed for their structural homogeneity, efficiency, sparsity, and overall performance. Among the models analyzed, the additive noise models yielded the most compact graphical structure, with the sparsification method revealing the optimal causal structure in the synthetic data provided by MPHIA. This analysis has practical implications for data privacy research related to healthcare.

In a specific magnet, called the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, researchers found that the transition from a stable to metastable phase happens through nucleation at the boundaries of the stable phase, resulting in unusual "flowers" that form on the metastable phase as it disappears. Contrary to what was expected, the transformation does not happen through the typical replacement of metastable skyrmions with stable ones through the process of bubble nucleation. Instead, the metastable phase gradually disappears from its edges and is replaced by a stable "flower" shape that creates sharp boundaries between the stable and metastable areas, resulting in complex mixing patterns of the stable magnetism with the residual metastable areas. Researchers found that the speed at which the metastable phase disappears is directly related to the difference in energy between the metastable and stable phases, as calculated based on the theoretical model of the material's behavior. They also developed a theoretical model that explains this entire process as a result of the gradual changes in the material's behavior as it cools.

High-dimensional time series data in numerous fields are now being analyzed.  In social network analysis, a high-dimensional influence model uses variables to calculate each individual's influence based on their behavior, such as online posts, throughout a given time period.  This influence can serve as crucial information for multiple purposes including forecasting future behavior, detecting anomalies, and classifying entities.  This paper introduces a variety of influence models, categorized by their focus: probabilistic, graph-based, spatial, and others.  This influence model classification provides insights into the numerous challenges in this field and offers recommendations for future research.

The paper offers a method for solving the balance problem by adapting the concept of stability from convex optimization. Specifically, it defines stability in the optimization framework and examines conditions for solution stability. By applying Lyapunov's principle, the research demonstrates that in the general case, balance is achievable only under strict stability. Furthermore, the paper establishes that when conditions of strong convexity are met, the solution to the balance problem is indeed stable. It also showcases balance's applicability to modeling the stability of walking and it is illustrated with simulations.

In various fields such as business, law, medicine, and surveillance, there is a growing need for automated image forensics that can detect whether an image has been digitally manipulated. One such forensics task known as reversible concealment detection requires not only determining the presence of hidden content but also localizing its area and uncovering its hidden form. Existing techniques for concealment detection are limited by their low accuracy and the absence of localization and content restoration capabilities. To address this, we propose a novel approach called the reversible concealment detector network (RCNet), which leverages the full capacity of deep neural networks and the uncertainty sampling techniques of Bayesian Neural Networks to significantly enhance detection accuracy. Experimental results show that our method surpasses the current best approach by a large margin and also achieves the lowest false positive rate in a large-scale dataset evaluation, while additionally achieving the top results for localization and content restoration.

Recent advancements in high-performance computing have enabled detailed three-dimensional simulations of global convective dynamos, covering a range of solar system objects and processes. These simulations, extending from small planets to stars and galactic dynamos, provide invaluable insights: they surpass previous theoretical and numerical limitations, and have successfully produced quasiperiodic magnetic activity in numerous scenarios. Analysis of these simulations reveals the substantial impact of turbulent effects, revealing complex interactions between influenced mean-field equations and magnetic dynamos. To accurately understand and replicate these findings, a comprehensive approach to turbulent influences within mean-field frameworks is essential, building upon traditional concepts. By expanding our understanding in this direction, future studies may unlock the secrets of global convective dynamos, paving the way for promising advancements in dynamo theory and related research areas.

A crucial aspect of galaxy evolution is the powerful cosmic outflows driven by active galactic nuclei (AGN) that help regulate star formation. It has been challenging to detect these outflows in galaxies other than the centralmost ones near the event horizon of the AGN due to a lack of sensitivity. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we successfully detected a massive molecular outflow in the nearby gas-rich galaxy NGC 4945. Our extensive ALMA observations found an extensive molecular emission spanning up to 2.4 kiloparsecs from the nucleus of the galaxy. Specifically, we observed a faint CO emission at a relatively low density of about 1000 solar masses per square parsec, indicating a massive total outflow of about 1.3 billion solar masses within a 13 percent confidence bound. Our findings suggest the outflow is likely being pushed by the AGN radio jet, indicating outflows can occur in galaxies with relatively high levels of starbursts. These discoveries imply the outflows may be a common phenomenon across various galaxy environments. A massive flow of gas is likely being pushed out of NGC 4945, indicating the extensive inflow of gas is being counteracted by the AGN driven outflow. It is likely the extensive starburst in the galaxy has triggered a starburst in the surrounding region, pushing the gas towards the center of the galaxy. The outflow is likely causing a decrease in gas available for star formation and

A key component in simulating complex plasmas is the kinetic equation that governs particle transport, which involves a quasilinear model driven by the drive of the electric field and a collisional mechanism that induces Gaussian fluctuations randomly. This study develops a conservative numerical approach based on the Galerkin method to solve the kinetic equation for fast particles, which describes laser interaction with plasmas. The approach uses a conservative numerical scheme for solving spatially dependent Fluctuation Distributions, which up to second order, is compatible with the original kinetic equation. It maintains the inherent conservation properties of the equation including its total energy. The numerical results indicate that the approximation is accurate with an order of O(Δx^2 + Δx^4), where Δx represents a spatial mesh size and shows promising potential for applications in petascale simulations of laser-plasma interactions.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative Generalised Adams-Bashforth methods have already demonstrated high order accuracy for order p variable stepsize methods with p ranging from 1 to 5, when applied to standard first-order differential equations. We now build upon this existing work by extending it to standard first-order differential equations. We investigate and evaluate new parameters for VSS BDF methods of order p from 1 to 5, further validating the previously established results from order 1 to 4 in a rigorous theoretical context, while achieving similar results for order 5 through theoretical argumentation based on its local error properties.

This study delves into the exponential stability of abelian c0-semigroups in Banach spaces, with a particular focus on the robustness of this stability. It is demonstrated that this robustness is achievable under specific Lyapunov conditions. Additionally, an example is provided to illustrate a situation where the robustness fails without these conditions being met.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a Python-based computational tool designed to calculate how dimuonium compounds interact with substances via chemical bonding, electromagnetic forces, and other interactions at ground state. MuMuPy generates molecular structure predictions, including the spatial arrangement of dimuonium compounds bound to a substance and various property predictions that are visualized graphically. MuMuPy incorporates a user-friendly interface with recommended parameter settings to simulate dimuonium compound interactions. MuMuPy also includes functions for simulating different treatment methods for dimuonium compound interactions. Additionally, it allows users to predict the behavior of dimuonium compounds in the presence of a single substance particle or multiple particles.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in two primary ways: total wealth and relative wealth. Total wealth indicates overall returns, while relative wealth showcases performance relative to a benchmark or average market. This paper develops an optimal portfolio theory grounded in power utility functions for total and relative wealth. Our key contribution is a comprehensive framework combining the Merton and Fisher models, thereby extending the classical mean-variance model. By using a dual approach, we derive our results, which show that optimal portfolios comprise a combination of the market portfolio and a zero-cost portfolio consisting of benchmark components. Our models can be applied to various scenarios, including benchmarks of various risks and with or without transaction costs.

The intergalactic medium holds crucial evidence of the formation and evolution of galaxies, including dwarf galaxies. A thorough investigation of IGMedium in dwarf galaxies is significant because it shares key characteristics with galaxies at low mass levels, mimicking cosmic conditions during the early stages of galaxy formation. Additionally, the IGMedium in dwarf galaxies offers insights into their unique star-forming episodes, which are thought to be driven by gas inflows. However, the nature and impact of these inflows remain unclear, largely due to a lack of knowledge concerning the IGMedium within these galaxies. This review primarily focuses on dwarf galaxies classified as Late-Typed (LTS) or Classic (LT) in the Milky way, although it may explore other systems when relevant. This study aims to provide a comprehensive review of IGMedium in dwarf galaxies, encompassing: 1) characteristics of IGMedium within these galaxies; 2) the relationship between IGMedium and their host galaxies; and 3) theoretical simulations of galaxy evolution, including the IGMedium within them. Ultimately, the review aims to summarize the current knowledge on IGMedium in dwarf galaxies and introduce future research pathways.

We're investigating the behavior of a two-dimensional fermionic model, the XXZ Heisenberg model, in the presence of local bosons. This model has previously been used to examine the failure of fermionic quasiparticles in novel materials. In the case where each site contains an even number of bosons, it's known that the model fails the fermionic quasiparticle property when a certain symmetry is broken. However, our research reveals that when each site has a finite number of bosons, breaking the U(1) symmetry by a finite magnetic field results in a more significant failure of this property for all low-energy quasiparticles, not just those with symmetry breaking. Moreover, our results demonstrate that this property can be restored in a certain regime for all quasiparticles, except those with specific high-spin properties. This highlights the importance of examining various physical systems to gain a more complete understanding of the failure of fermionic quasiparticles.

We examine the divergence properties for variations of the Thompson groups and braided Thompson groups and establish that certain normalized homomorphism varieties have non-divergent behavior under specific conditions, including for $G_4^s$, $G_4^s\times\mathbb{Z}$, and the braided Thompson groups. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient criteria for the divergence of $G_m^s$ and demonstrate divergent behavior for the full Thompson group $F$ under specific metrics.

This project focuses on using the Complete RAG framework developed by Facebook for answering open-ended questions. Our approach leverages this method, which combines document retrieval with question-answers, to create a comprehensive model for generating answers. In a retrospective analysis, we examined the effectiveness of several key configurations within the RAG framework and made two primary modifications to further enhance our model's performance. Firstly, we implemented a more targeted approach to generate answers by filtering output based on relevance to the original question. Secondly, we improved the efficiency of document filtering during the training process by increasing the number of filtered documents. In a series of experiments, we evaluated the impact of various RAG configurations, particularly with regards to the number of generated tokens and additional neural layers, as well as our proposed enhancements. Our results reveal that this approach leads to substantial improvements in both the accuracy and efficiency of open-ended question-answering models.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a logarithmic weight given by $\frac{1}{(1-x)^{\alpha}}$, with $\alpha$ being a positive real number. A specific weight function with a singularity at $x=1$ is considered. Using the Riemann-Hilbert and the nonlinear steepest descent methods, the solutions in the critical regions $|x| \to \infty$ show distinct asymptotic behaviors for different signs of $x$. Moreover, a conformal mapping is employed to determine the asymptotics in the polynomial's unit disk, with $\alpha$ being a parameter that affects the degree of the logarithmic weight's singularity. Various weight functions with real-degree singularities can be obtained by setting $\alpha$ within a specific interval $0 < \alpha < 2$. Specifically, three cases are derived: $\alpha$ equal to 1, 0.5, and 0.6667, illustrating the applicability of the method for different weights with real-degree singularities.

Utilizing Microtasks on Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire human-generated annotations is widespread in natural language processing. Nonetheless, the quality of these annotations is contingent upon various factors, primarily the expertise and attention to detail of the assigned workers. To optimize the hiring process, we have established a rating system that selects and assigns annotations from experienced workers with a proven track record in summarization. Our analysis of 1,192 annotations from 61 workers reveals that our proposed method effectively identifies and leverages the most skilled workers, thereby ensuring high-quality annotations. Moreover, we investigate how annotation quality can be further enhanced by providing detailed instructions, demonstrating the importance of clear guidelines in this context.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting nuanced spatial-temporal video representations being a major area of study. Current approaches typically leverage pre-trained vision transformers to generate a unified video representation, but this is constrained to handling temporal information alone. Moreover, the invariant nature of transformers enables self-attention at any level, but this is not adequately harnessed to capture token-specific representations relevant to the retrieval task. This study introduces the Token Shift and Choice Transformer Network (TS2-Net), a more sophisticated variant of the v5t that leverages multiplexing and channel-specific attention to both depth and width to produce highly detailed representations of text and video. Through the integration of shift and choice modules, the TS2-Net is designed to unlock highly tunable token-level interactions and adaptiveness, enabling the retrieval of semantically coherent video clips based on the input text. Extensive evaluations on benchmark datasets reveal the superior performance of TS2-Net over current state-of-the-art approaches.

We investigate how a hypothetical neutral current exists at the tree level in a specific two-top quark, one-lepton configuration and, based on unitarity constraints, derive a limit on the neutral current's strength that does not exceed 4.1 times 10^-5. This limit is derived from the correlation between the transverse missing energy and the largest lepton energy observed in 139 fb^-1 worth of luminosity from pp collisions at 13 TeV.

In research on network analysis, a new category of hybrid networks has been introduced that blend simple uniform attachment with a preferential attachment mechanism. These networks maintain a balanced proportion of weak and strong links, similar to small-world networks, while also shifting towards a more targeted distribution of strong links over time. They exhibit growth patterns that transition from an initial phase with a slow growth rate to an later phase characterized by accelerated growth. The metrics used to measure their evolution show a noticeable transformation from small-world networks to a more targeted network structure.

The proliferation of wireless services is causing increased interference in critical systems, leading to a need for early detection of disturbance sources. We propose an automated framework for identifying the type of wireless disturbance encountered by a sensor, which would inform mitigation measures to prevent system failure. We have collected a large dataset of wireless signals representing various disturbance types and used it to train a convolutional neural network model. Our approach demonstrates high accuracy across multiple disturbance classes. Notably, it can detect the presence of disturbances and identify their types in just a few received samples, outperforming existing techniques.

To investigate the interactions of particles and antiparticles in cosmic string spacetime, a novel model involving a interaction between a Klein-Gordon particle and the energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field is developed. The principle tasks are to compute the thermodynamic properties of the observed spacetime, determined by a scalar field with a lagrangian describing a mix of regular and space-time displaced Bessel fluids. The interactions of particles and antiparticles, influenced by vorticity, electric charge, and the gravitational influence of a cosmic string, are established by a interaction term in the Klein-Gordon equation. The interactions and correlations of particles and antiparticles, affected by the above mentioned physical factors, are established by a interaction term in the Klein-Gordon equation. The interactions and correlations of particles and antiparticles, influenced by the gravitational influence of a cosmic string, are established. The analysis shows how the gravitational influence of a cosmic string modulates the interactions and correlations of particles and antiparticles, resulting from a interaction term in the Klein-Gordon equation, in the presence of a cosmic string.

A nonatomic, locally normal measure algebra represents a significant relaxation of the criteria for a measure algebra to be called discrete. We establish in this paper that a locally normal measure algebra necessarily has a countable base if it exhibits countable local divisibility, thus resolving the discrete-local-divisibility conjecture for measure algebras. We further demonstrate that the requirement of countable local divisibility can be substituted with the condition of countable generation. Consequently, this result yields the truth of the local divisibility-conjugacy dichotomy in groups and other related structures.

We propose a novel observable in Deep-Inelastic Scattering (DIS) off nuclei that can help establish the presence of Deep-Inelastic Scattering (DIS) at large $x_B$ by identifying the Recoil Proton Alignment (RPA) in exclusive neutral pion production. The Displaced Velocity Vector (DVV) method is used to develop this new observable which emerges due to the longitudinal recoil proton momentum acquired from the created $\rho$-meson in the spirit of the parton-to-parton scattering hypothesis for DFCS. By considering the parton-to-parton scattering in the framework of QCD, its all-order QCD calculation is presented along with implications for possible experimental verification at JLab 12 GeV. We present detailed calculations using our global QCD analysis with various momenta scales, comparing the new RPA observable with the existing RSS from rhegion's recoil alignment and show that in the kinematic range of our example $X_B=0.25$, $Q^2=2$ GeV$^2$, $P_e=9$ GeV the new RPA is about two times larger than the RSS. While each of these alone may not be large enough to establish DFCS at large $X_B$, their combination provides a crucial test for identifying large-$X_B$ CLC calculations in the case when experimental data on $d\sigma/DVV$ is positive. The proposed RPA can be measured at JLab 12 GeV

This foundational analysis establishes the theoretical framework for a sub-set of Artificial Intelligence systems, which we have termed 'Enhanced Artificial Intelligence' (E-AI). A fundamental concept underpinning E-AI is 'Digital Humanoid Conscience' (DHC), an original idea used to model human-like reasoning within this class of systems. Key characteristics of E-AI include its integration of multiple forms of intelligence, such as biological and hybrid intelligence, which must be governed by a distinct form of intelligence to ensure optimal operation. We define three types of operational governance: rule-based, network-based, and network-centered. To address both practical and theoretical security risks associated with these systems, which we have designated as 'Trojan PC', we propose a set of protocols for system security. Our primary objective in developing this conceptual framework for E-AI is to provide a universal understanding of this field and establish international cooperation to advance E-AI research and development.

Our research involves examining the superfluid transition in an optical lattice featuring bosonic molecules with intrinsic spin-orbit coupling. Due to these molecules' unique intrinsically spin-orbit coupled characteristics, the superfluid transition exhibits a diverse range of behaviors compared to systems without, as evidenced by the occurrence of a number of new phenomena. Notably, the superfluid transition is characterized by a shift in critical temperature in response to non-modulated and modulated potential shapes, as well as varying internal states of superfluctuation. Furthermore, the application of a local disturbance on both unmodulated and modulated superfluids demonstrates the emergence of novel many-body states, particularly metastable triplerons, which can influence the superfluid transition. Through the use of a quantum Monte Carlo simulation, the impact of spin-orbit coupling on the superfluid transition in systems with strong correlations is thoroughly investigated.

Consider a finite abelian group $G$ of rank $r$ and denote its dual by $\widehat{G}$. 
Let $T$ be a subset of $\widehat{G}$ consisting of a single element or two elements of odd multiplicity, 
and a finite number of elements with even multiplicity less than or equal to $r$. 
We can associate a graph $G_{T}$ to $G$ and $T$ such that its vertex set corresponds to the subset $\widehat{G} - T$, with two vertices connected by an edge if their difference has a value within $T$. 
The study focuses on the properties of these graphs when they are non-degenerate and connected, with emphasis on their topological structure and relation to degenerate graphs. 
We establish a classification of these graphs up to isomorphism based on a specific factor group and demonstrate that every such graph can be derived from a rank-one graph through a specific operation that preserves the degree of each vertex. 
Furthermore, a comprehensive topological description of these graphs is given in terms of simplicial complexes, with the proof also showing that every degenerate graph has a specific representation using a finite abelian group and two vectors from its vertex set.

Quantum gravity theories are likely to be prominent in understanding nature, yet exactly solving multi-loop integrals in anti-de Sitter space, a crucial part of this endeavor, has proven unfeasible. Despite significant efforts, no complete solution has been achieved, whereas significant progress has been made in four-dimensional situations compared to lower dimensional ones. In this research, we introduce a new approach in two-dimensional conformal gauge theory to calculate integrals up to the second loop, using a simplified type of supergravity solution. Inspired by its success, we also examine the properties of this gravity theory and discover intriguing features, resolving long-standing problems, such as the AdS/CFT duality conjecture in two-dimensional cases. This new method is expected to be expanded to higher loops and to the presence of additional variables, potentially shedding light on the presence of "ghost" modes, a long-standing enigma in AdS/CFT studies.

This research paper undertakes a comprehensive examination of Gaussian Process kernel derivation.  It seeks to establish a fundamental framework from which these derivatives can be understood.  The work is motivated by the realization that the primary sources of Gaussian Process models are often obscure or inaccessible to the broader field.  The present study provides a straightforward mathematical derivation of three fundamental kernel types - linear, logarithmic, and exponential - and discusses their potential applications in model development.  Additionally, the paper explores two structured kernel types - linear and logistic - along with presenting examples to illustrate Gaussian Process modeling in multi-modal function regression.

The forthcoming muon colliders face a unique challenge resulting from beam-induced background radiation, which arises from beam losses, collisions, and machine errors. In the form of gammas, RF pulses, scintillators, and electromagnetic simulations, various strategies to manage this noise have been explored, including passive shielding, active shielding, and optimization techniques such as data augmentation and filtering. A newly developed strategy, the "Muon Collider Electronics System" (MCES), has also been proposed, integrating the Volcano strategy with data acquisition and conditioning technologies to improve detector capability to identify signal from noise. A software model known as "Software Beam Induced Background Radiation" (SBIBR) has been created to simulate the behavior of beam-induced background radiation, facilitating the evaluation of different methods to manage this noise and the development of a unified solution applicable to both detectors and sub-detectors.

Prominent approaches to neural network sparseness, such as pruning, have drawn attention in recent years. However, due to their non-differentiable nature, they necessitate approximations when applied in combination with backpropagation, resulting in considerable training overheads. This paper proposes Spartan, a new method for inducing sparseness in neural networks through a conveyance-based regularization technique that is fully differentiable. Spartan's flexibility enables it to be used in a variety of sparseness-promoting strategies and can even approximate existing methods with precise control over hyperparameters. Spartan's effectiveness is illustrated through experiments on a range of tasks, including training Sparsnet, a neural network architecture inherently designed for sparseness, and transferring knowledge from pre-trained models on different datasets. Furthermore, Spartan is shown to enhance the interpretability of neural networks by encouraging organized activation patterns across multiple related tasks.

According to the Anderson-Mermin-Nirenberg theorem, gauge symmetry has no bearing on the phase of a system with multiple gauge redundancies. Nevertheless, the phenomenon of an emergent anomaly occurs in a system with no genuine symmetries, resulting from artificial conservation laws created by redundancies in the gauge formalism. In the context of ultracold bosons interacting via short-range repulsive forces, and confined in a torus-shaped potential well with hyperbolic boundaries, we uncover an issue with gauged symmetries that originates from the non-gaugeted conservation law of angular momentum. Upon gaugetizing the momentum, a 'Pauli obstruction' arises when the system reduces to a topologically trivial state of repulsive one-dimensional bosons. This barrier can be overcome by connecting it to either another one-dimensional system or a two-dimensional system with a finite number of fermions.

Previous studies indicated that software developers may not always prioritize reliability and functionality over "bugs" introduced by inexperienced or inexperienced managers. The goal of this research was to understand the frequency and magnitude of so-called 'test odor', which arises when non-technical individuals interfere with software testing, causing confusion and leading developers to doubt the reliability of test results. The study collected responses from over 261 active OpenStack developers and found that nearly 85% of those surveyed estimated the impact of test odor as substantial, with over 75% suggesting it would take at least two hours per module to rectify test odor, with some developers reporting it could take up to 80 hours. The study's findings are the first to quantitatively measure so-called 'test odor', providing empirical data from the perspective of software developers. The results may influence future quality management strategies within software projects.

This study investigates the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a significant class of nonlinear, time-varying differential-inclusion problems, encompassing both convex and non-convex cases, through the implementation of a sweeping procedure.

We introduce KKMCee, a revised version of the CERN-EP Monte Carlo generator for lepton colliders, specifically designed to simulate lepton and quark pair production in these colliders. This tool builds upon the established KKMC generator, incorporating two distinct photon coupling correction procedures: Photon Pair Production Correction and Photon-to-QED Correction. These corrections are applied in consecutive steps to ensure the accuracy of final simulation results. This paper outlines the underlying physics processes, implementation details, and example simulations provided by KKMCee.

Measuring the inter-beat interval provides valuable information about a person's heart health. This measurement can help identify early signs of specific conditions, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and distinguish between different types of heart conditions, like atrial fibrillation. Unfortunately, relying on electrocardiogram intervals alone is not always enough to make an accurate diagnosis due to their susceptibility to noise and minor inaccuracies. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel method using the Tiramisu model to refine inter-beat interval assessments. By applying this new approach, we have achieved significantly reduced error rates and improved reliability.

We have developed a novel random approach for approximating the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD). The method builds upon existing stochastic singular value decomposition (SVD) techniques for matrices and has been extended to accommodate tensors of arbitrary order. Our approach calculates an approximate factorization of the tensor A, represented as A ≈ U˜∑V˜, which involves determining the approximately singular matrices U˜ and V˜ and an approximate matrix ∑˜ containing the dominant tensor singular values and associated vectors. Our randomized technique for tackling the problem of tensor SVD has been proven to converge under certain conditions at a rate determined by the condition number of the tensor A and the number of stochastic passes made. Our method for tackling tensor SVD generates a consistent set of approximate right-singular matrices V˜ and corresponding left-singular vectors, allowing the computation of an approximate low-rank approximation of a tensor A. Our approach for tackling tensor SVD involves calculating an approximate factorization of the tensor A, which has been demonstrated to be effective in denoising applications involving compressed tensors and image renovation.

Real-world networks are often dynamic and influenced by various internal and external factors, resulting in constant changes to their structure. Effective analysis and prediction in these types of networks require a representation that captures the entire timeline of evolution. To this end, a novel node embedding framework is introduced that incorporates temporal relationships in multiple types of evolving graphs. This framework utilizes an enhanced version of the GCN model, incorporating temporal information from diverse perspectives, and can handle the distinct characteristics of various graphs with a single model. Our approach enhances the performance of current state-of-the-art node classification and link prediction algorithms. Thorough evaluation of the proposed framework is performed using real-world graphs from different domains, indicating its efficiency and effectiveness.

Our analysis with a p+7H scattering model from Phys. Rev.
